stories.title: Govt to strengthen requirements for data centre incident reporting
stories.summary: Malaysian authorities are drafting enhanced mandatory incident reporting requirements for data center operators, mandating prompt notification to government agencies when digital infrastructure disruptions occur. The proposed framework aims to improve national cybersecurity resilience and critical infrastructure protection by reducing information asymmetry between operators and regulators during outage events.
stories.why_it_matters: Operators face expanded compliance obligations and potential liability exposure, particularly given ambiguity around what constitutes 'prompt' reporting and which disruption thresholds trigger mandatory notification. The regulatory development positions Malaysia between Singapore's mature critical infrastructure framework and Indonesia's lighter-touch approach, with implementation quality determining whether reporting requirements become genuine risk management tools or checkbox exercises that delay operational response during actual incidents.

stories.title_zh: 政府将加强data centre事故报告要求
stories.summary_zh: 马来西亚当局正在起草对数据中心运营商的增强强制事件报告要求，规定数字基础设施中断发生时必须及时向政府机构通报。拟议框架旨在通过减少 outage 事件期间运营商与监管机构之间的信息不对称，提高国家网络安全韧性和关键基础设施保护。
stories.why_zh: 运营商面临扩大的合规义务和潜在责任风险，特别是考虑到'及时'报告的定义以及哪些中断阈值触发强制通报存在模糊性。这一监管发展使马来西亚处于新加坡成熟的关键基础设施框架和印度尼西亚较轻触方法之间，实施质量将决定报告要求是成为真正的风险管理工具还是在实际事件中延迟运营响应的勾选练习。
stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 12): The government is looking to strengthen reporting and notification requirements for data centre operators to ensure disruptions affecting digital infrastructure can be promptly communicated to the relevant authorities.

Digital Minister Gobind Singh Deo said a proper notification mechanism should specify the nature of the incident and measures, whether the problem could be resolved, and the sectors potentially affected. Such requirements are increasingly important as more industries and economic activities become reliant on data centre infrastructure and uninterrupted digital services, he added.

“If there is a flood that results in damage to the data centre and there is no mechanism today that requires the data centre to notify anyone or an authority who can be notified. If you have an ecosystem where the entire country, or a substantial part of it, is reliant and dependent on data centres, and there are problems, you need to start thinking of how you govern infrastructure,” he told reporters after the launch of the National AI Readiness Week 2026, here Thursday.

Gobind said the Data Centre Task Force (DCTF), co-chaired by him and Minister of Investment, Trade and Industry Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani, was also examining challenges arising from the industry’s rapid expansion. He said the government was also exploring ways to encourage data centre investors to develop supporting energy and water supply infrastructure to meet the industry’s growing requirements.

He stated that recent investment announcements by Google went beyond data centre development to include efforts to build the supporting ecosystem in Malaysia. “So if we are going to look at substantial demands and requirements for energy as we go ahead, we are also starting a discussion around whether you can look at these companies building energy supplies to run the data centres, and also water supplies to do the same,” he said.

Commenting on Malaysia’s 27th place among 70 countries in the IMD World Digital Competitiveness-related AI ranking, he said the focus should now shift towards ensuring investments in AI infrastructure generate tangible economic benefits. “Ultimately, the question is whether or not we can see returns on those investments,” he added.

stories.title: Chinese AI firms rush to secure Nvidia chip capacity as spy scandal stirs fear of US curbs
stories.summary: Chinese artificial intelligence companies are accelerating efforts to secure access to Nvidia chip capacity through cloud providers and leasing arrangements, driven by fears that a recent espionage scandal involving the company's CEO could trigger expanded US export controls. The scramble reflects deep uncertainty about whether Washington will restrict remote access to advanced GPUs currently available through overseas cloud instances.
stories.why_it_matters: The preemptive capacity hoarding risks creating artificial shortages and price spikes in global cloud GPU markets, disrupting AI development timelines for non-Chinese customers. If Washington does extend restrictions to cloud-based access, the bifurcation between Chinese and Western AI infrastructure would accelerate dramatically, forcing Chinese firms toward domestic alternatives like Huawei's Ascend chips and potentially fragmenting global AI research collaboration.

stories.content:
The companies worry Washington may tighten restrictions on their remote use of advanced processors

\[BEIJING\] Chinese artificial intelligence companies are trying to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity at data centres outside China, concerned that a scandal involving the US chipmaker’s chief executive Jensen Huang could spur Washington to tighten restrictions on their remote use of advanced processors, three people familiar with the matter said.

The moves underline concern among Chinese technology companies over the potential closing of a gap in US export controls.

Seeking to protect US dominance of the critical sector, Washington restricts exports to China of Nvidia’s most advanced artificial intelligence chips, but Chinese companies can access such processors remotely by renting computing power at data centres overseas.

A major Chinese cloud provider has discussed internally whether to lock in overseas Nvidia chip capacity, while some companies have contacted data centre operators about reserving it, the people said.

The people declined to be identified, or to identify the cloud provider because of the sensitivity of the matter.

Smaller AI labs are considering similar steps, including approaching major providers of rented computing power in South-east Asia, two of the people said.

The companies fear the controversy surrounding Huang could add political momentum to the Remote Access Security Act, or Rasa, a US bill that would give the Commerce Department authority to regulate remote, cloud-based access to restricted technology, the people said.

The House of Representatives passed the bill in January by a 369-22 vote, and it awaits Senate action.

Advanced Nvidia processors are used to train and run the large AI models behind chatbots and other generative AI products.

Restricting overseas cloud access would make it harder for Chinese developers to obtain high-end computing power without importing the chips directly.

Huang said on Sunday (Nov 8) that he had been unfaithful to his wife.

*The New York Times* reported that the woman involved was Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based cloud-computing company Megaspeed, and that US authorities had concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset.

Reuters could not independently verify that allegation, which China has denied.

Alice Huang had business dealings and investment ties with several leading Chinese technology companies, including Tencent and Alibaba, according to two people familiar with the matter. Tencent and Alibaba did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Singapore business filings show that Alibaba subsidiary Apex Enterprise Solutions provided financing to Speedmatrix, a Malaysian company linked to Megaspeed, according to records reviewed by Reuters.

Megaspeed has faced scrutiny over suspicions that it helped Chinese customers gain access to advanced Nvidia chips subject to US export controls. The company has denied illegally diverting chips to China.

Nvidia, Megaspeed and the US Commerce Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

## Grey market buying

The prospect of tougher enforcement has also fuelled demand for restricted Nvidia AI chips in China’s grey market, prompting traders and intermediaries to start stockpiling these processors, two of the people said.

They said buyers fear the controversy could prompt a broader US crackdown on smuggling of advanced chips and AI servers into China.

A Chinese university with deep ties to the People’s Liberation Army bought Nvidia’s powerful H200 AI chips in October despite being on a US export blacklist, procurement records show, highlighting gaps in Washington’s efforts to curb China’s access to advanced technology.

US prosecutors in March charged Super Micro Computer co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw and two others with conspiring to divert servers containing Nvidia chips to China through a South-east Asia-based company.

Prosecutors said the company bought about US$2.5 billion of servers from Super Micro between 2024 and 2025, and that a substantial portion was diverted to China. The defendants have not been convicted. REUTERS

stories.title_zh: Singapore：data centre行业处于'转型阶段'，Aprea的John Lim表示
stories.content:
This article first appeared in The Edge Malaysia Weekly on November 2, 2026 - November 8, 2026

ONCE a niche sector in institutional real estate portfolios, data centres are now emerging as the fastest-growing sector in global real estate and infrastructure investing, driven by demand for cloud computing and AI. However, supply and demand concerns have risen, as market observers question whether the scale and pace of data centre investment will be supported by sufficient demand and revenue to justify the funding committed.

Despite this, John Lim, chairman of JL Family Office and Asia Pacific Real Assets Association (Aprea), remains optimistic, believing any near-term oversupply could be absorbed as adoption grows. He points out that data centres are not new — the first generation, buildings fitted with air-conditioning and equipment, has been around for about four decades, but has changed significantly over the past 12 months.

“We still use the term ‘data centre’, but the new generation is very different. These facilities need power, water, grid connections and sophisticated machines to support generative and agentic AI. That is driving growth in the sector. From a real estate practitioner’s perspective, however, every new asset class attracts investors who jump on the bandwagon, potentially creating oversupply. The question is whether demand will catch up,” says Lim at the media briefing of the Asia Pacific Real Assets Leaders’ Congress 2026 in Tokyo.

He adds that there are two schools of thought — one sees oversupply creating market challenges. At the same time, the other believes that as AI continues to grow, today’s excess capacity could become tomorrow’s undeveloped, which is a cycle already seen in office, retail and student housing sectors.

“I think we are at that transition stage. As a real estate professional, I cannot yet say how it will play out or whether we will see a bubble burst. As a layman, however, I believe AI will continue to grow. If that view is correct, the current oversupply and capital-raising challenges will be a short-lived period,” says Lim.

On funding, Lim highlights three typical pools of capital: private equity, sovereign wealth funds and public markets, which include real estate investment trusts (REITs). He emphasises REITs, believing they will play an increasingly important role by giving retail investors access to the sector and effectively allowing end users to participate.

Aprea CEO Sigrid Zialcita concurs, adding that funding is becoming a concern among industry players, given the substantial capital required. Anecdotally, some insurers have pulled back from financing the sector, while rising capital costs are adding pressure, she adds. This makes REITs increasingly important, as placing stabilised assets into a REIT allows owners to release capital for further investment.

Political opposition to data centres across both major US parties is also weighing on sentiment. But market signals are mixed — two major IPOs, Blackstone-backed AirTrunk and Nvidia-backed Firmus, have been postponed, while SoftBank-backed DayOne is going ahead and seems well received. “We are still trying to understand how this will unfold, but investors on our platform are increasingly highlighting funding constraints,” says Zialcita.

To date, infrastructure and private equity are still dominating the sector. By the end of 2025, infrastructure funds accounted for about half (57%) of the total US$155.9 billion (RM632 billion) equity value in data centre investments tracked by MSCI, with private equity contributing another third. In contrast, real estate funds accounted for less than 10%.

Over the next few years, Lim is keeping watch on data centre counters, given the substantial pools of public-market capital in Japan, China, Australia and Singapore. “Overall, I am more optimistic than pessimistic. Some people believe the sector will be oversupplied and demand for generative AI will fall. But new asset classes often go through the same cycle — rapid investment, consolidation and renewed growth. The key question is whether demand disappears, and I do not believe it will,” he adds.

Across Asia-Pacific, cloud adoption, the AI buildout and shortages of power and land are forcing developers to rethink how these buildings get financed, built and valued, says Zialcita. Launching Aprea’s new publication, Wired to Grow: Asia’s Data Centre Reckoning, she adds that Asia-Pacific is set to add 24 gigawatts (gw) of data centre capacity between 2025 and 2030, roughly US$286 billion of real estate value. Operators may also need another US$486 billion for graphics processing units (GPUs) and networking gear.

Demand drivers are also shifting. Cloud computing remains the foundation of data centre demand, while AI is creating higher power densities and new requirements for cooling and electrical infrastructure. However, Aprea’s research suggests that AI inference demand will be driving the bulk of workloads by 2030, not training, says Zialcita.

AI training refers to the initial learning phase where a model studies datasets to recognise patterns and adjust its internal weights. At the same time, AI inference is the active operational phase, where trained models use fixed weights to analyse new data or make predictions. Zialcita explains that while training needs scale and big campuses where power and infrastructure can be assembled in bulk, inference needs proximity to end users to keep latency down.

Developers are also prioritising sites with existing or expandable grid capacity, access to transmission infrastructure and substations, credible connection timelines, and sufficient land to support large campuses.

Singapore boasts connectivity, regulatory clarity and an established ecosystem that allows it to continue to attract capital. However, constraints on power, land and new supply limit the pipeline of investable opportunities. These constraints are supporting activity in neighbouring Johor, which has emerged as a major data centre market, supported by greater land and power availability, lower development costs and spillover demand from across the causeway, says Zialcita.

Citing DC Byte’s 2026 Global Data Centre Index Report, Zialcita points out that Johor tops Asia-Pacific’s data centre metro markets, followed by Sydney, Shanghai and Tokyo. “Johor has benefited immensely from Singapore’s moratorium on data centre development. Although the moratorium has been lifted, development costs in Singapore remain exceptionally high, driving investment in large, power-hungry facilities,” she adds.

Singapore’s influence extends beyond hosting data centres. Its companies are behind some of the region’s biggest deals, including Singtel’s partnership with KKR on a US$5.1 billion acquisition.

As such, Zialcita believes capital is flowing where it makes economic sense, and these transactions demonstrate the financial heft of Singapore players, even as development takes place elsewhere.

Meanwhile, Lim says Johor ranks highly in the index largely due to its cost advantages and available power. Singapore’s policies have also encouraged data centre development to shift towards Malaysia, reflecting the view that such facilities generate relatively limited economic value for the land they occupy.

“The Johor government, supported by the sultan, is very, very supportive of all this. There are a lot of incentives. However, I think the most sophisticated data centres will never go to Johor. They will come to Japan or other developed countries. Investors might consider Johor for mid-tier data centres, weighing the policy incentives against the reliability of some resources,” adds Lim.

Japan, with its large, sophisticated digital economy and political stability, is emerging as one of Asia-Pacific’s most active markets for direct investment in data centres. The Far East stands out in recent transaction activity — according to MSCI, data centre transactions have reached US$11.6 billion since 2024. JLL Research also found that the country’s data centre market size reached US$23.4 billion in 2024, with growth projections for 2025-2030 indicating an annual average growth rate of 6.7%, reaching US$33.4 billion by 2030.

“Three of the five recent direct investment transactions were in Japan, and those include the US$997 million acquisition of Colt DCS Keihanna by CapitaLand Ascendas REIT and Mitsui. In fact, according to MSCI, Japan was the second-largest destination for data centre investments globally, after the US. This is how important Japan is,” she adds.

Institutional investors are accepting yields of around 4.3%-4.5% in Tokyo and Osaka, compared with nearly 8% in Beijing and Shanghai, says Zialcita. Japan’s sophisticated digital economy, political stability and tenants with strong credit profiles help explain investors’ willingness to accept these lower yields, she explains.

Beyond Tokyo and Osaka, the country’s southwestmost island, Kyushu, and northernmost island, Hokkaido, are attracting operators seeking additional power and geographic diversification, Zialcita says. Known as Japan’s “Silicon Island”, Kyushu benefits from semiconductor fabs such as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. Singapore-headquartered DayOne Data Centers, for instance, plans to develop a new data centre campus in Imari City, Kyushu’s Saga Prefecture, with 200 megawatts (mw) of grid power.

The campus will be developed in phases on a site of more than 133,000 sq m within the Imari East Industrial Park, with support from Saga Prefecture and Imari City. The development includes 160mw of secured power and land. The initial phase is targeted to begin operations in 2030.

Hokkaido also offers abundant land, significant renewable energy potential and a naturally cold climate that helps reduce data centre cooling costs. SoftBank and its subsidiary IDC Frontier are building a large-scale AI data centre in Tomakomai City, the fourth largest in Hokkaido. The centre will serve as a core facility for SoftBank’s “Brain DataCenter” concept — part of its next-generation social infrastructure initiative aimed at decentralising data processing and energy consumption nationwide.

Scheduled to begin operations in fiscal 2026 (ending March 2027), the Hokkaido Tomakomai AI Data Center is expected to become one of Japan’s largest, with an area of 700,000 sq m and a power capacity exceeding 300mw.

stories.title: Singapore: Data centres get a reality check
stories.summary: Singapore's data center investment climate has cooled markedly, evidenced by AirTrunk's postponed S-REIT IPO and Firmus Grid's stalled public market debut. The setbacks reflect investor reassessment of yield expectations, power availability constraints, and the sustainability of premium valuations in a market where regulatory capacity controls have tightened supply dynamics.
stories.why_it_matters: The capital markets retrenchment threatens to constrain development funding for planned capacity expansion, potentially widening the gap between approved projects and financially viable construction starts. For Singapore specifically, the IPO postponements test whether the city-state can maintain its position as a data center financialization hub alongside its operational hub status, with regional competitors like Kuala Lumpur and Jakarta potentially capturing capital flows if investor sentiment persists in favoring less regulated, higher-growth markets.

stories.content:
This article first appeared in The Edge Malaysia Weekly on November 2, 2026 - November 8, 2026

PUBLIC capital’s yearning for data centres has cooled considerably. On Oct 13, Bloomberg reported that AirTrunk’s S-REIT initial public offering (IPO), scheduled for the Singapore Exchange this year, had been “postponed”. On Oct 8, Firmus Grid, an Australian artificial intelligence (AI) and data centre company, postponed its IPO on the Australian Securities Exchange.

In the US, CoreWeave, a neocloud that has borrowed heavily to rent out AI computing power, saw its bonds sink in the week of Oct 12 to 16 while the cost of insuring CoreWeave’s debt against default hit a record. Oracle, which has borrowed heavily to invest in data centres, saw its debt rated one notch above junk.

Data centres, the power- and water-guzzling infrastructure necessary for the AI revolution, have proved less successful in seeking public capital after years of private funding.

Singapore-headquartered DayOne Data Centers is weighing options for its US IPO, including a potential delay or size cut, as volatility around data centres increases, according to a Bloomberg report. While DayOne has been waiting for the right window to launch the IPO, it has also been considering the possibility of pushing back the share sale until the market recovers, Bloomberg claims. Other options include going ahead with a smaller listing that may raise US$2.5 billion (RM10.14 billion) to US$3 billion, the report adds.

In 2023, when Singapore’s Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) temporarily lifted the moratorium on building data centres, its first Data Centre — Call for Application (DC-CFA) pilot awarded 80mw to four entities: GDS Holdings, AirTrunk-Bytedance, Equinix and Microsoft. Of the four, the GDS-backed entity, renamed DayOne in 2025, and AirTrunk are seeking exits via IPOs.

Interestingly, IMDA’s second DC-CFA awarded 50mw of capacity each to four entities that were either listed or backed by a large corporate: Keppel, Equinix, Digital Realty and ST Telemedia.

DayOne’s sole data centre in Singapore will be ready next year. In its Form 1 lodged with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, the GDS Holdings-backed company says DayOne has built campuses at two locations in Johor — Nusajaya Tech Park and Kempas Tech Park — and claims to have secured about 1.4gw of bookings by bringing in five “global” hyperscalers. In Batam, DayOne is developing two campuses, Nongsa Digital Park and Kabil Industrial Tech Park. GDS Holdings is listed in Shanghai.

Controversy continues to dog data centre developers. On Oct 13, the BBC reported that 300 residents on Batam were furious that the taps at home had run dry, while the data centres in the new Nongsa Digital Park seemed to have enough water to protect their machines from overheating, highlighting the negative aspect of the rush to build data centres in communities that were not ready.

Separately, in September, Nasdaq-listed Oracle issued a force majeure notice to a unit of Blue Owl Capital for Project Jupiter to shield itself from rising costs and delay rent payments if the project misses its 2028 operational target. Project Jupiter is a US$165 billion data centre campus in New Mexico. By invoking force majeure, Oracle aims to defer full rent payments (potentially by up to three years) if the site fails to launch on time in 2028, shifting carrying and delay risks back to Blue Owl and its lenders rather than walking away from its role as the anchor tenant.

In July, the New Mexico State Land Office rejected an application by Oracle for the “Green Chile Project”, a 27.4km natural gas pipeline extension needed to supply energy to the data centre site’s fuel cells.

Mayank Srivastava, CEO of Singapore-headquartered developer and operator of data centres BDx, notes that the well-being of communities near data centre developments was not sufficiently considered. “Specific to the case of data centres, probably there wasn’t enough awareness about the impact on communities, and in the initial days, developers just went wherever there was surplus power, and then when the data centres kept expanding in those locations, the power supply had to be upgraded. Nobody was really thinking about aligning costs and incentives, and as it would happen, the costs were passed out of the community, which is not a fair thing to do in the first place, and that is why you saw a lot of community resentment.”

Project Jupiter also encountered intense pushback from state and local officials over massive water consumption, carbon dioxide emissions and a lack of direct state revenue generation. On Oct 14, Oracle proposed an Energy Service Agreement with El Paso Electric to pay US$100 million over 10 years to support affordable electric rates for New Mexico customers.

“Communities need to be engaged, and the incentives, such as costs, need to be aligned properly. If an enterprise is coming up to set up a factory, the cost for setting up that factory has to be allocated proportionately. For instance, if a factory is coming up which needs the power infrastructure to be upgraded, then the cost of that upgrade should be borne by that factory,” Mayank observes.

At the forefront of the data centre value chain are operators and owners looking for investors. Some have tapped the local retail investing community, while others have tapped accredited and institutional investors through private equity and debt, and of course bank loans.

This year, the excitement in the air that AirTrunk’s S-REIT was set to be the largest IPO has abated because of its seemingly expensive pricing. Although officially headquartered in Australia, AirTrunk had clinched the IMDA’s first DC-CFA with joint-venture partner ByteDance. AirTrunk was sold to Blackstone and the Canada Pension Plan in December 2024.

However, on Oct 3, the Australian Financial Review reported that AirTrunk’s scheduled A$4.4 billion (RM12.5 billion) IPO could be postponed due to stock market volatility, the tech and AI sell-off and surging borrowing costs.

Separately, on Aug 18, DayOne, which is still loss-making, with a US$369 million net loss in FY2025 (the company has a December year end) for ordinary shareholders, and a US$82 million net loss in 1HFY2026, tapped the three local banks for a green loan for its data centre in Singapore. DBS Bank, Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp (OCBC) and United Overseas Bank (UOB) announced that DayOne had secured a four-year, S$530 million (RM1.68 billion) green loan from them to support the development of its first data centre in Singapore.

In December 2025, DayOne announced a mezzanine financing facility of €500 million, expandable up to €1 billion upon mutual agreement, from Brookfield and a global sovereign investor for data centres in Finland. And on Oct 13, DayOne tapped more banks for a syndicated loan for its Johor data centres.

In July last year, when DayOne broke ground for the Singapore data centre, which will be completed next year, it had signed a power purchase agreement with Sembcorp Power, under which all operations will be fully covered with renewable energy, and a research and development partnership agreement with the National University of Singapore (NUS) to advance data centre innovation as part of the Sustainable Tropical Data Centre Testbed Phase 2.0 (STDCT 2.0) initiative.

DayOne’s transactions, coupled with a growing debt pile, come amid rising global demand for digital infrastructure, driven by the rapid adoption of AI, cloud computing and 5G technologies.

At Data Centre World Asia held in late September, DayOne executive vice-president Ong Kok Chye noted at a forum that not a week goes by without a huge mega announcement of contracts worth tens of millions of dollars for data centres and AI financing.

“If you just look at this conference, it used to occupy maybe one or two floors. Now we have the entire building in just a few years and we see all kinds of people coming to this conference,” Ong said, referring to the four floors of Sands Expo & Convention Centre occupied by Data Centre World.

“We used to have operators, vendors at Data Centre World. Now we have bankers, lawyers, all kinds of people. It goes to show how interconnected this industry is, and the amount of money pouring into it is incredible. If you look at the second-quarter announcements of all the hyperscalers combined, they are spending almost US$800 billion just this year alone,” Ong continued.

That may sound rosy, but who’s doing the paperwork and financing? Ong wondered. On the other hand, oil prices are above US$100, which feeds into inflation. The US Federal Reserve has recently raised interest rates by 25 basis points to 3.75%-4%. The 30-year yield on US Treasuries reached 5.67%, a 25-year high on Oct 7.

“At the same time, projects are getting bigger. There are new markets to explore; markets like Malaysia and Thailand, which people didn’t really talk about, are now very much on everyone’s mind. How is the finance industry in those markets coping to handle this huge demand for onshore management? And we also have new categories of customers such as neocloud, which are very popular with customers,” Ong said.

In a forum titled “How financing models are changing to fuel data centre expansion”, Jean Monson, managing director of the investment banking division at MUFG, asked whether there is enough financing to meet demand. “In August, a couple of reports were released. One report estimated the amount needed over the next three years to finance the AI factory at US$7 trillion. If we break it down, you have US$2 trillion to US$3 trillion going to graphics processing units (GPUs), and the remainder goes to power, land, the grid, among others. Everyone thought that was a staggering number until the following week when another report released cited the figure as US$23 trillion. These numbers get revised constantly, and we are definitely seeing numbers in the trillions,” she said.

Financing 1gw of a data centre costs around US$2.4 billion for the core and shell, US$3 billion for the power infrastructure, US$1 billion for network and cabling, US$1.6 billion for the cooling system and upwards of US$21 billion for servers and chips.

Monson estimated the GPUs could cost between US$50 billion and US$60 billion. The two largest transactions financed by MUFG totalled US$60 billion, comprising US$40 billion and US$20 billion of loans. These numbers used to take years to reach. “We’re seeing the same amount happen in a matter of months, of double-digit billions of financing that can close within a matter of months. I think the question has really been: ‘Is there going to be enough supply to finance all of this?’” she pondered.

The kind of data centres that are used by hyperscalers and AI campuses are calling for billions of dollars, Digital Realty senior director of acquisitions and investments Rebecca Ng confirmed. “The cheque size is getting longer, but bigger, and the timeline from development to stabilisation is also getting longer for this type of large-scale investments, and that is changing the way the sector is thinking about financing these large-scale developments,” she pointed out.

Capital with a higher appetite for risk should finance land acquisition, entitlements and the availability of power and water, Ng observed. Often the very early part of data centre development financing is done by private equity and debt, including bank debt.

“Then you get to stabilised assets, which is where usually capital gets recycled, and then you get to the core investors, which are the REITs, the long-term owners of stabilised core assets,” Ng said.

Traditionally, data centres were valued as real estate or industrial estate, Ng noted. Discounted cash flow models are used to value investment properties based on their operating cash flows, outlook for rentals, outlook for expenses including interest cost, and these were discounted back to net present values using a discount rate that is affected by risk-free rates including 10-year and five-year sovereign bond yields, and the outlook for interest rates.

“Increasingly, as cheque sizes grow and limited partners (LPs) begin to understand more about the industry, we are seeing a lot of different fund structures, such as companies asking for different kinds of co-investments, or asking for longer holds for assets that require longer development through poor periods. From a developer perspective, customer contracts or anchor tenant leases are starting to become financing instruments, where it’s a milestone in construction financing,” Ng explained.

Meanwhile, Digital Realty is increasingly turning to private market tools such as development joint ventures, private funds and capital recycling, Ng added.

For example, in March this year, Digital Realty formed a US$3.25 billion US hyperscale data centre fund with global institutional investors, including public pensions, sovereign wealth funds, endowments and foundations, corporate pensions, insurance and asset managers, and family offices.

Digital Realty retains a 20% stake in the fund, focused on owning and developing hyperscale data centres in US Tier-1 metros, including Northern Virginia, Santa Clara, Dallas, Atlanta, Charlotte and New York. Additionally, a Digital Realty-Blackstone joint venture developing 10 data centres was announced in December 2023.

“So you spread the capital requirements and the risk as well. I think in Apac we see less of the developer joint venture because the markets are so diverse, and you see more localised joint ventures with local partners to take into account the local nuances, the local capital hurdles and the risk appetites,” Ng said.

Mayank of BDx says data centre financing is predicated on the customer who will sit inside the data centre. “We build data centres to be factories, so the data centre financing is predicated on the customer who is coming into the data centre to put their compute and so on,” he says.

He sees data centres as part of the AI value chain, which he terms AI factories.

The main risk for data centre development is capital availability. In the early years, capital for data centres and AI was aplenty. Increasingly, though, capital providers are becoming more discerning, as evidenced by the failed IPOs of Firmus and AirTrunk. The rationale for the IPO yield of 6.5% to 6.7% is that it is significantly higher than Singapore’s fixed deposit rates and Singapore’s 10-year Singapore bond yield. However, S-REIT investors are reluctant to pay such a yield.

Investors are increasingly aware that a sponsor headquartered in Australia, with a portfolio in Asia-Pacific, will have a cost of capital that blends different risk-free rates. First, Australia’s risk-free rate is closer to 4.6% and not 2.4% as in Singapore. Second, although the data centres are in Singapore, Australia, Tokyo, and Johor, the racks, pipes, generators, transformers, fibre-optic cables and water-cooling systems are priced in US dollars. The US risk-free rate, which is the global risk-free rate, is 5.2% to 5.3%. And data centres are built to last more than 20 years. But the equipment inside has different lifespans. With the current crop of data centre S-REITs, investors are familiar with depreciation and capital expenditure in relation to data centres, to keep them current or future-proof them.

Sajal Kishore, managing director and head of EMEA & Apac infrastructure and project finance at Fitch Ratings, explained that the greenfield and development phase is usually funded by private money and banks. “You would get a negative carry during that phase, and also the banks are pluggable for the asset, to monitor the progress,” Sajal says.

Once the data centre is de-risked, the owners can tap the capital markets with the long-term issuances. Issuers then have the option of going for asset-backed securities (ABS), commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) or project finance, Sajal indicates.

“We have been involved across different groups in all these three different formats. It’s a market that I believe is still fairly well serviced by the banks at the moment. But the transactions that come to us are the better-quality assets because in capital markets, there have been very limited amounts of cold call issuances in the data centre world,” he says.

The best credits for data centres are those driven by hyperscaler transactions. On the other hand, sponsor quality is getting quite mixed, Sajal adds. “Neoclouds (AI-first cloud providers) have a business model that may not be that strong; their credit quality tends to be quite weak compared to the hyperscalers, which introduces a counterparty risk. Then you have this whole rush of data centres, the cryptocurrency guys, data miners, all trying to repurpose their data-mining holds into a data-centre operation. Inherently, these assets are located in more remote locations because they really don’t need to be in a strong location and that makes them challenging,” he further explains.

The most valuable data centres are those used for cloud features in financial hubs, inferencing and storage in important economic locations such as Singapore.

“As a ratings agency, we really look at cloud and inference (for ratings purposes),” Sajal adds.

Rating agencies are not likely to consider data centres used as AI training facilities beyond the initial contract.

“We will not look at contract renewal. These are unlikely to merit a recontract because they’re usually in remote locations, and also the counterparty needs to weigh in on the overall project rating. Cloud and inference are a lot more robust and location plays a very strong role,” he reasons.

“The most interesting aspect of financing that has happened this year is that the equipment that sits inside of the data centre is becoming an investable asset class. Nvidia’s GPUs, for instance, have exchanges trading compute futures. That means these chips are becoming more and more financeable,” Mayank points out.

Previously, Nvidia’s GPUs struggled to get financed. “That hump has been crossed. The other part, which has contributed to the hump being crossed, is the fact that AI today is generating real revenues. So people like OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Alphabet are seeing serious revenue accretion because of AI being deployed,” Mayank says.

In August, Nvidia signed memorandums of understanding (MOUs) with Apollo Global Management, Blackstone, BlackRock, Brookfield Asset Management, Goldman Sachs and KKR to establish financing platforms for Nvidia’s customers, “mobilising” more than US$500 billion third-party capital for hyperscalers, frontier AI labs and enterprises to build out data centres and acquire Nvidia hardware. “Recently, more than US$500 billion was committed by the big six asset managers for Nvidia. So, there’s a lot of private money which is already in, and we are seeing now public money is beginning to get very comfortable with AI factories,” Mayank says.

Why are investors so confident? Financial institutions are profiting from AI models.

“The guys who are creating the AI make money out of it from people like us, where AI is being created, so the data centres find it a lot easier to get financing done,” Mayank adds.

During a media briefing on Sept 22, UOB global head of wholesale banking Frederick Chin said its involvement in a US$3.1 billion senior syndicated term loan is the first time such a structure has been done for GPU financing in Southeast Asia.

“We have done two GPU financings in this region. One was bilateral and smaller. This is the largest US$3.1 billion syndicated loan (for Zankore). The intent is to get broader participation. This is cash flow-driven lending, and we are quite confident this deal will set the benchmark and start creating liquidity for more such deals,” Chin says.…

stories.title_zh: Siemens上调中期展望，AI驱动的data centre需求推动订单增长
stories.content:
ZURICH (Nov 12): Siemens on Thursday reported better-than-expected results in its fourth quarter and lifted its mid-term growth outlook, as strong demand for trains and from AI-related data centres continued to boost orders.

The German engineering group, whose products range from trains to electrical gear for factories, buildings and data centres, said industrial profit jumped 22% to €3.89 billion (US$4.31 billion) in the three-month period ended Sept 30.

The figure, the highest ever posted by Siemens, beat forecasts for €3.71 billion in a company-compiled consensus of analysts.

Revenue rose 11% to €23.68 billion, exceeding forecasts of €23.39 billion, while orders surged 58% to a record €34.77 billion.

The jump in orders was largely fuelled by large contract wins at Siemens' Mobility divisionand its Smart Infrastructure business, which supplies data centres.

Siemens said it was seeing "sharply higher' order intake in its electrification and electrical products businesses, including large contract wins from data centre customers mainly in the US and Europe.

Power distribution equipment, cooling gear and digital simulations of facilities are among the products that Siemens provides for data centres.

As a result, Siemens raised its mid-term outlook and now expects comparable annual revenue growth of 7%-11%, up from its previous forecast of 6%-9%.

For 2027, it expects revenue to increase by 9-11%, towards the upper end of its target range.

Shares of Siemens were up 4.4% in early trading in Frankfurt.

Siemens also gave details on its plans to reduce its stake in Siemens Healthineers, saying it planned to distribute one Siemens Healthineers share for every two Siemens shares held by shareholders, confirming a *Reuters* story on Wednesday.

Under the plan, Siemens would transfer 34.1% of its stake to shareholders, taking its holding down to around 33%. In the mid-term, Siemens plans to sell down its stake to below 20% and hold Siemens Healthineers as a financial investment.

stories.title: Schneider Electric details liquid cooling orchestration for AI data centers
stories.summary: Schneider Electric has outlined how liquid cooling orchestration software helps AI factories manage cooling infrastructure. This aims to improve GPU utilization, operational efficiency, and reduce costs in high-density AI deployments.
stories.title_zh: Schneider Electric详述AI数据中心liquid cooling编排方案
stories.content:
Schneider Electric has detailed how liquid cooling orchestration software is becoming essential for high-density AI deployments. The company highlighted that increasing AI rack and chip heat fluxes necessitate direct liquid cooling.Liquid cooling orchestration software coordinates cooling towers, chilled water plants, chillers, computer room air handlers (CRAHs), facility cooling loops, and cooling distribution units (CDUs). This software-driven approach continuously anticipates cooling demand and matches capacity, helping to minimise operating costs and improve system efficiency.The orchestration software provides a consolidated view of performance across multiple data centre locations. This allows operators to identify best practices and standardise operations.For AI factories, liquid cooling is now a thermodynamic necessity rather than a design choice, according to Schneider Electric. The challenge is to orchestrate cooling infrastructure at scale to optimise cost, efficiency, resilience, and GPU utilisation.Orchestration manages cooling as a system, ensuring capacity efficiently matches AI workloads and minimises waste. It can deliver cost savings by improving power usage effectiveness (PUE) and water usage effectiveness (WUE).The software also helps optimise data centre design and construction costs by providing accurate data on power and water needs. It transforms cooling from individual assets into a coordinated thermal management platform.By maintaining required heat rejection and thermal headroom, operators can maximise GPU performance and improve cooling-capacity utilisation. This reduces unnecessary energy or water use.The software ingests real-time telemetry from both liquid and air-cooling infrastructure, offering a unified operational view. This is crucial for hybrid thermal architectures common in AI environments.As AI factories expand, cooling optimisation becomes a fleet management consideration. The software provides a centralised view of thermal performance and efficiency across sites, enabling benchmarking and best practice standardisation.Cooling orchestration software uses AI to make intelligent cooling capacity decisions for GPUs. It monitors real-time GPU and rack power telemetry as a leading indicator of heat load.Predictive AI models anticipate workload-driven thermal demand and proactively adjust CDU and chilled water plant setpoints. This ensures cooling capacity is in place before heat reaches the coolant loop.Managing the full heat transfer chain as one system allows operators to run warmer supply temperatures and gain more economiser hours. It also cuts pumping energy and recovers stranded cooling capacity without compromising thermal resilience or GPU performance.Liquid cooling orchestration can also extend beyond day-to-day operations. It provides greater visibility into actual cooling requirements and performance across sites.This helps operators optimise capacity, identify best practices, and make more informed infrastructure investments. It can avoid unnecessary capital expenditures and reduce operating costs, supporting efficient and scalable AI infrastructure.

stories.title: NetApp unveils Novus architecture for AI factories
stories.summary: NetApp has introduced Novus, a new data architecture designed to support AI factories. This architecture aims to meet the demanding data needs of AI infrastructure providers, ensuring optimal GPU utilization.
stories.title_zh: NetApp发布面向AI factory的Novus架构
stories.content:
NetApp has unveiled Novus, a new data architecture aimed at supporting AI infrastructure providers operating environments. This architecture is designed to help AI factories maximise the efficiency and utilisation of millions of graphics processing units (GPUs).A single GPU may require up to 2GB/s of data throughput to remain fully utilised, according to NetApp. Meeting this demand at scale requires infrastructure capable of delivering enormous data volumes at sustained speeds.
### Novus architecture details

NetApp Novus exceeds 100TB/s of aggregate throughput and can keep hundreds of thousands of GPUs productive, said Arindam Banerjee, Chief Platform and Technology Officer, NetApp. The architecture separates metadata and data into independently scalable planes. It then unifies thousands of storage nodes behind a single namespace.Mr. Banerjee added that Novus is architected with standards-based pNFS/NFS access through supported Linux client environments. This aims to remove a major source of recurring overhead. It also preserves a single namespace for shared, multi-tenant AI infrastructure.NetApp CEO George Kurian stated that Novus is designed to bring the proven security, resiliency, quality-of-service, and multi-tenancy foundations of ONTAP into a single architecture. Providers can keep tenants isolated, workloads predictable, and GPUs productive even when thousands of jobs compete for the same data plane.
### Economic impact for AI factories

GPUs represent one of the largest capital investments in an AI factory, according to NetApp. Their economic value depends on how effectively they are used. When GPUs wait for data, expensive computing capacity sits idle. This can translate into substantial financial exposure across tens of thousands of accelerators.Storage performance is no longer merely a technical consideration; it is an economic variable. It directly influences the productivity of AI infrastructure and the returns on its capital investment. NetApp Novus aims to transform efficiency, utilisation, and profitability for Neocloud operators, hyperscalers, and GPU-as-a-Service providers.

stories.title: How the world became too reliant on Jensen Huang
stories.summary: The CEO’s travails are a reminder that a single point of failure is never a good thing for a big company
stories.title_zh: 世界如何变得过于依赖Jensen Huang
stories.content:
The CEO’s travails are a reminder that a single point of failure is never a good thing for a big company

A WAYWARD CEO is a major problem for any company. The scandal unfolding at the top of Nvidia, though, is a liability for a much broader set of people. It’s a good moment to think about how to make the world less dependent on the fortunes and foibles of Jensen Huang.

The Nvidia chief said on Nov 8 that he had been unfaithful to his wife, following reports that a woman with whom he had relations may have been a Chinese intelligence asset.

Given the value of Nvidia’s intellectual property and the fraught nature of US-China politics, this raises countless questions that a board probe, assisted by outside lawyers, will have to investigate.

Whatever they find, it is undeniable that Nvidia without Huang as its CEO would have a problem. He is already spread thin, overseeing about 60 direct reports, with no obvious successor. And the company’s board is not exactly robust.

Its directors have an average tenure of 18 years, more than twice the S&P 500 mean, according to consulting firm Spencer Stuart. Five of them have served for roughly three decades, with no apparent resistance from shareholders.

What hurts Nvidia hurts the market because of its sheer size. The US$4.5 trillion company makes up nearly 7 per cent of the S&P 500.

But Huang’s empire has also underwritten growth at many of its customers, taking stakes, backstopping loans, and financing data centre builders who in turn host artificial intelligence labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic. Huang was a cheerleader when tech investors lost their nerve – most recently during the so-called SaaSpocalypse software sell-off.

Fortunately, there are plenty of templates for reducing dependency on a CEO.

Companies such as Morgan Stanley, Amazon and Apple made successful chiefs into chairs while successors found their footing. Look too at Google DeepMind founder Demis Hassabis, who just stepped back from his role as CEO to instead become chair, giving him more space to think about the AI big picture.

Even if Nvidia isn’t prepared to countenance Huang leaving his CEO post, many companies have de facto number-two spots – presidents and chief operating officers, say – that ensure investors know there’s someone on hand if the boss collides with a bus. Nvidia should do that too.

It’s also time to think about whether the oversight foisted on banks – long regarded as essential social infrastructure – should apply to big tech companies. Lenders such as JPMorgan, with regulators breathing down their necks, have no choice but to build in contingency plans.

Nvidia is nowhere near as complicated as a Wall Street bank, but it is becoming similarly systemic. It would not be a surprise to see that on the new Congress’ agenda in 2027.

Investors already seem to be contemplating a less Nvidia-centric world. Shares in rival AMD rose 12 per cent on Monday; upstart chipmaker Cerebras was up 5 per cent.

Customers move more slowly than markets, but Huang’s slip-up gives them, too, a prod. Whatever the consequences, his predicament is a helpful reminder that a single point of failure is never a good thing. FINANCIAL TIMES

stories.title: AI infrastructure reliability starts before rack arrives
stories.summary: Data centre operators must focus on manufacturing quality and traceability for AI infrastructure. The reliability of integrated AI racks is increasingly determined in the factory, not just on-site.
stories.title_zh: AI基础设施可靠性始于机架到达之前
stories.content:
Stephen Draper-Garcia, a data centre expert for the UK and Ireland at Desoutter Tools, states that manufacturing quality and traceability are crucial for supplier assurance in the AI era.He explains that integrated AI infrastructure arrives with significant manufacturing and assembly work already completed. This means a data centre's eventual reliability is partly determined before the rack reaches the facility.
### Traceability and procurement

Traditional quality assurance focuses on final testing, which confirms a product worked when it left the factory. However, traceability provides visibility into the manufacturing process itself.A detailed manufacturing history can link a serial number to information such as production sequence, assembly results, operator records, and any rework events. This data helps operators understand how a specific unit was built.As AI infrastructure investments increase, manufacturing assurance is moving into procurement conversations. Buyers are now examining how products are manufactured, including whether records can be associated with individual units.They also assess if critical operations were completed within specification and how process changes are controlled during production volume increases. Suppliers' ability to demonstrate consistent quality control throughout production is becoming a key evaluation factor.
### Investigating issues

When equipment develops an issue in service, manufacturing records can help investigate the cause. This information can trace affected equipment back to a particular production period or component batch.It also identifies whether other units share a similar manufacturing history, warranting further investigation. This data supports fault isolation and corrective action throughout the equipment's operational life.Data centre operators need confidence that critical processes are controlled, results are attributable to individual products, and exceptions are visible. For suppliers, demonstrating controlled, repeatable, and transparent processes with verifiable evidence is increasingly important as infrastructure complexity and production volumes rise.

stories.content:
Tenant expansions at two California data centres lift portfolio occupancy to 97.5%

\[SINGAPORE\] NTT DC Real Estate Investment Trust (Reit) on Wednesday (Nov 11) posted a distribution per unit (DPU) of US$0.0432 for the first half of FY2026/27, 10 per cent above its initial public offering projection of US$0.0393. Net property income (NPI) exceeded forecasts and net finance costs came in lower than expected.

For the six months ended Sep 30, distributable income stood at US$45 million, against the projected US$40.9 million.

NPI was 4.9 per cent above projection at US$55.8 million, while gross revenue came in 2 per cent higher at US$119.8 million. The stronger NPI was attributed to increased tenant fit-out revenue, lower real estate taxes and favourable foreign exchange movements.

Net finance costs were also 5.5 per cent below projection at US$10.4 million, mainly due to lower interest rates.

The Reit’s leasing performance improved during H1, with portfolio occupancy by information technology load rising 1.6 percentage points to 97.5 per cent as at Sep 30, from 95.9 per cent three months earlier.

The increase was largely driven by expansions secured at its CA1 and CA3 data centres in California. Most of the leases commenced in September and are expected to contribute a full quarter of rental revenue from Q3 FY2026/27 onwards. Including leases signed but yet to commence, committed occupancy would rise to 98.1 per cent.

The Reit recorded rental reversion of 11.7 per cent during H1, largely driven by a 23 per cent rental reversion from the renewal of its SG1 NTT Master Services Agreement in the first quarter. It also secured lease renewals with a monthly base rent of US$903,000.

As at Sep 30, the portfolio’s weighted average lease expiry stood at four years, with 11.2 per cent of leases due to expire in the current financial year ending Mar 31, 2027.

The Reit’s aggregate leverage fell to 29.9 per cent as at Sep 30, from 31 per cent at end-June. Total debt stood at US$528 million, while the weighted average all-in interest rate declined to 3.8 per cent from 3.98 per cent.

Some 68.4 per cent of the Reit’s borrowings are on fixed rates, and it has no loan maturities until FY2028/29. Its existing loans also come with two 12-month extension options.

Separately, unitholders approved changes to the management fee structure on Nov 6. Under the revised arrangement, the performance fee will be linked to year-on-year DPU growth instead of NPI, with the new structure taking effect from FY2026/27.

The fee will be calculated at an annual rate of 0.1 per cent of deposited property if DPU growth exceeds 3 per cent but is below 5 per cent, and 0.2 per cent if growth is at least 5 per cent. DPU growth is calculated before accounting for the performance fee but after accounting for the base fee.

Units of NTT DC Reit fell 2.2 per cent or US$0.02 to close at US$0.90 on Wednesday, before the announcement.

stories.summary: [SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Nov 12):
stories.title_zh: 关注股票：新航、CDL、Sats、AEM、StarHub、NTT DC Reit、SBS Transit、Centurion
stories.content:
\[SINGAPORE\] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Nov 12):

Singapore Airlines (SIA) : The national carrier posted net profit of S$209.7 million for its second quarter ended Sep 30, up from S$52.4 million in the previous corresponding period. This was due to stronger operating profit and a lower share of losses from associate Air India. Revenue rose 14.3 per cent to a record S$5.6 billion, while operating profit rose 16.3 per cent to S$463.7 million from a year earlier. For the first half of FY2026, SIA’s net profit fell 43.9 per cent to S$133.9 million year on year. The board declared an interim ordinary dividend of S$0.02 a share and an interim special dividend of S$0.05 a share, bringing the total payout to S$0.07 a share. Shares of SIA closed 0.4 per cent or S$0.03 higher at S$7.17 on Wednesday, before the news.

City Developments Limited (CDL) : The property group said it expects to post a “significantly weaker” financial performance for its second half ending Dec 31. Certain capital-recycling deals that the group had earlier expected to materialise in the rest of FY2026 are now expected to be completed in FY2027, it said in a business update on Wednesday. The group is also currently undertaking valuations of its property portfolio, which it noted “may give rise to impairment losses”. Shares of CDL closed 1.2 per cent or S$0.09 lower at S$7.12 on Wednesday, before the update.

Sats : The air cargo handler and airline caterer posted a 2.8 per cent rise in net profit to S$81.1 million for its second quarter ended Sep 30, from S$78.9 million in the previous corresponding period. This was due to higher cargo and meal volumes and lower tax expenses, even as the Middle East conflict raised input costs and disrupted operations, it said on Wednesday. Earnings per share stood at S$0.054 for the quarter, up from S$0.053 the year before. Revenue for the quarter rose 9 per cent to S$1.71 billion, from S$1.57 billion. Shares of Sats closed 2.6 per cent or S$0.10 higher at S$4 on Wednesday, before the news.

AEM : The semiconductor equipment maker’s net profit surged more than 18-fold to S$73.4 million for the nine months ended Sep 30, from S$4 million a year earlier. Revenue rose 57.2 per cent to S$452.1 million on stronger demand for semiconductor testing solutions. AEM raised its FY2026 revenue guidance to S$680 million to S$705 million, from S$630 million to S$680 million, and its earnings per share guidance to S$0.30 to S$0.33, from S$0.245 to S$0.275. Shares of AEM closed 3.1 per cent or S$0.21 higher at S$7.05 on Wednesday.

StarHub : The telco reported a 26.3 per cent dip in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) to S$72.1 million for the third quarter ended Sep 30, from S$97.8 million the prior year. Revenue rose to S$486.8 million, up 4.5 per cent from S$464.8 million previously. The telco said that despite rising revenue, Ebitda continued to decline because of lower gross profit, higher operating expenditure and lower income from other avenues. Shares of StarHub ended flat at S$1.04 on Wednesday.

NTT DC Real Estate Investment Trust (Reit) : The Reit on Wednesday posted a distribution per unit of US$0.0432 for the first half of FY2026/27, 10 per cent above its initial public offering projection, as net property income exceeded forecasts and net finance costs came in lower than expected. For the six months ended Sep 30, distributable income stood at US$45 million, against the projected US$40.9 million. Net property income was 4.9 per cent above projection at US$55.8 million, while gross revenue came in 2 per cent higher at US$119.8 million. Units of NTT DC Reit fell 2.2 per cent or US$0.02 to close at US$0.90 on Wednesday, before the news.

SBS Transit : The public transport operator posted a 35.5 per cent rise in net profit to S$19.6 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30, from S$14.5 million in the previous corresponding period. This was due to a S$13 million write-back of prior years’ Fuel Equalisation Fund provisions, which was included in the operating profit. Operating profit for the quarter rose 37.7 per cent to S$22.6 million, from S$16.4 million in the year-ago period. Revenue fell 1.1 per cent to S$382.1 million from a year earlier due to a lower bus service fee from the loss of the Tampines package, as well as lower rail grants and ridership. Shares of SBS Transit closed flat at S$3.56 on Wednesday.

Centurion : The accommodation provider reported a 35 per cent rise in revenue to S$280.1 million for the nine months ended Sep 30, from S$208.3 million in the previous corresponding period. This was mainly due to the consolidation of Westlite Mandai and new operational beds in Singapore, as well as its Harum Megah portfolio in Malaysia and Epiisod Macquarie Park in Australia. Revenue for the third quarter ended Sep 30 rose 41 per cent to S$95.2 million, it said in a business update. Shares of Centurion fell 2.4 per cent or S$0.03 to close at S$1.21 on Wednesday.
