stories.title: Google funds USD $160 million water plant in Negeri Sembilan
stories.summary: Google is financing a $160 million water treatment facility in Negeri Sembilan, Malaysia, designed to produce 65 million liters of treated water daily for both community use and its forthcoming Port Dickson data center. The shared infrastructure model represents a novel approach to addressing data center water consumption concerns in a region experiencing periodic water stress.
stories.why_it_matters: The dual-use water plant establishes a community benefit framework that may become template for hyperscale operators facing local opposition over resource consumption, converting data center water demand from competitive extraction to shared infrastructure investment. For Malaysia's water-stressed regions, however, the 65 million liter daily commitment raises questions about allocation priority during drought conditions and whether Google's financial participation sets precedent for other industrial water users to contribute equivalently to public supply augmentation.
stories.title_zh: Google 出资 1.6 亿美元在 Negeri Sembilan 建设水厂
stories.summary_zh: Google正在资助马来西亚森美兰州一个1.6亿美元的水处理设施，设计日产6500万升处理水，供社区使用和其即将建成的Port Dickson数据中心使用。这种共享基础设施模式代表了在周期性水资源紧张地区解决数据中心水消耗问题的新方法。
stories.why_zh: 这种双用途水厂建立了一个社区利益框架，可能成为面临当地反对资源消耗的hyperscale运营商的模板，将数据中心水需求从竞争性提取转化为共享基础设施投资。然而，对于马来西亚水资源紧张的地区，每日6500万升的承诺引发了干旱条件下分配优先权的问题，以及Google的财务参与是否为其他工业用水用户同等贡献公共供应扩充树立了先例。
stories.content:
Thu, 12th Nov 2026 (Today)
Google will fund USD $160 million in shared water infrastructure in Negeri Sembilan, tied to its planned data centre campus in Port Dickson.

The project includes an off-river storage reservoir and a water treatment plant, to be built with state authorities and water utility SAINS, with Gamuda as contractor.

Once completed, the facilities will be owned by Menteri Besar Negeri Sembilan and are expected to supply 65 million litres of treated water a day. The output is intended to serve both Google's future site at Springhill Industrial Park and broader public demand across the state.

The reservoir, along the Linggi River, is designed to capture excess river flow and rainfall during periods of high yield. The stored raw water will then be channelled to the treatment plant for domestic and commercial use. The reservoir is also intended to reduce flood pressure in nearby flood-prone areas.

During drier periods, the plant will be able to draw on stored reserves rather than rely on direct river flow. Google said this would support a steadier local supply without disrupting the river's natural flow.

The announcement adds detail to Google's digital infrastructure plans in Negeri Sembilan, covering the data centre campus, utility connections and workforce programmes. It will also pay for all electricity used by the campus and the direct infrastructure costs needed to connect it to the grid, subject to local rules.

State officials described the investment as part of a broader effort to attract long-term digital infrastructure spending while ensuring benefits for local communities.

"Google's planned data center campus represents an important milestone in Negeri Sembilan's journey toward becoming a competitive destination for high-value digital infrastructure investment. It demonstrates how private investment and public interests can be aligned from the outset to deliver sustainable, long-term benefits for the state and its people. We value Google's responsible and forward-looking approach, from the strategic selection of its development site to its commitments toward water infrastructure, power infrastructure upgrades, and the creation of new skilling and employment opportunities. These efforts demonstrate the importance of investors working in partnership with the State Government to address infrastructure requirements while delivering tangible benefits to the local community. For Negeri Sembilan, attracting investment is not simply about the size of the capital committed, but also about the quality of investment, its long-term economic contribution, and its ability to create value for our people. Google's presence also strengthens Negeri Sembilan's position as an emerging destination for the digital economy, with the potential to attract complementary investments, expand business opportunities for local companies, and support the development of a more skilled workforce. We see this as an opportunity to build a broader digital ecosystem that contributes to the state's long-term competitiveness," said Dato' Haji Najmuddin Sharif bin Sarimon, Chief Executive Officer, Invest Negeri Sembilan.

### Water and power

Google linked the water scheme to its broader environmental and infrastructure agenda in Malaysia. It said the Negeri Sembilan funding reflected its global target to replenish 120% of the freshwater volume it consumes, even though its own assessment found local water sources were not at high risk of scarcity or depletion.

"Google's decision to fund shared water infrastructure in Negeri Sembilan reflects our global ambition to replenish 120% of the freshwater volume we consume, even as our water risk assessment showed that local water sources were not at high risk of scarcity or depletion. This underscores our responsibility to grow our presence sustainably-pairing advanced digital infrastructure development with water replenishment projects, power infrastructure enhancements, and programs designed to upskill local talent for new career opportunities. We look forward to continuing our close collaboration with the State Government and local partners from construction through to long-term operations to deliver lasting value for the local workforce and community," said Drew Byrnes, Director and Head of Global Infrastructure and Energy, Asia Pacific, Google.

Alongside the water investment, Google said it has been working with consortiums led by Shizen Energy-Solarvest and TotalEnergies to add new clean power to Malaysia's national grid through power purchase agreements. Developers use these agreements to secure financing for new generation projects, including utility-scale solar farms.

### Skills push

Google is also expanding its work with SOLS Foundation on clean energy education and workforce training for young people. One initiative will place a Solar and Energy Lab in participating public schools, with each lab including a 2.56-kilowatt-peak solar array and 5.4 kilowatt-hours of battery storage.

Teachers will be trained to use the labs in lessons and co-curricular activities, with the aim of introducing younger pupils to solar technology and showing older students pathways into clean energy jobs. The systems are also expected to cut school electricity bills and provide backup power during outages.

A second programme will create a 36-hour training track within the SOLS Solar Academy for young people from lower-income backgrounds and Indigenous communities. The course is intended to support entry into trades such as solar photovoltaic installation, electric vehicle charging station maintenance and energy system operations, with job placement after graduation.

Google said the additional training would focus on digital tools increasingly used in clean energy work, including solar system sizing, load calculations, inverter and grid monitoring, and field reporting. It described the move as part of a longer-term effort to build a labour pipeline for Malaysia's energy transition as digital infrastructure expands.

Local utility SAINS said the new treatment and storage assets would strengthen the state's supply system for residents and businesses.

"As Negeri Sembilan's water utility provider, our priority is to safeguard the long-term dependability and quality of the state's public water supply. Google's proactive funding for new state-of-the-art water harvesting and treatment facilities serves as an exemplary model for public-private collaboration. The resulting 65 million liters of daily potable water capacity will strengthen the local supply system for residents and commercial users alike, ensuring Negeri Sembilan's water resources grow in tandem with the digital economy," said Dato' Ir. Haji Mohd Yazid bin Ahmad, Chief Executive Officer, Syarikat Air Negeri Sembilan.

stories.title: Australia considers mandatory registration and new operating controls for data centres
stories.summary: The Australian Energy Market Commission's final rule mandates technical performance standards for large inverter-based loads, specifically targeting data centers connecting to Australia's National Electricity Market. The standards aim to prevent cascading disconnections during grid disturbances by requiring fault ride-through capabilities and voltage response behaviors from facilities exceeding certain capacity thresholds.
stories.why_it_matters: Data center developers must now incorporate advanced grid-stabilization engineering into facility designs, increasing capital costs but reducing operational risk of mandatory curtailment during system emergencies. The rule establishes a precedent for treating hyperscale loads as active grid participants rather than passive consumers, with potential replication across other NEM jurisdictions and influence on standards development in New Zealand and Southeast Asian liberalized markets.
stories.title_zh: 澳大利亚考虑对数据中心实施强制登记和新运营管控
stories.summary_zh: Australian Energy Market Commission的最终规则强制要求大型inverter-based loads的技术性能标准，特别针对连接到澳大利亚National Electricity Market的数据中心。该标准旨在通过要求超过特定容量阈值的设施具备fault ride-through能力和电压响应行为，防止电网扰动期间发生级联断开。
stories.why_zh: 数据中心开发商现在必须将先进的电网稳定工程纳入设施设计，增加资本成本但降低系统紧急情况下强制削减的运营风险。该规则确立了将hyperscale loads视为电网主动参与者而非被动消费者的先例，可能在其他NEM司法管辖区复制，并影响新西兰和东南亚市场化市场的标准制定。
stories.content:
Australia’s energy market regulator is considering mandatory registration and new operational requirements for large data centres and other major electricity users, as it seeks to improve visibility of their power consumption and manage the impact of rapid changes in demand on the national grid.

The Australian Energy Market Commission (AEMC) **published a consultation paper on 12 November** in response to a rule change request from the Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO). The request identifies gaps in the National Electricity Rules (NER), which AEMO says do not currently provide it and network service providers with consistent visibility of large inverter-based loads (IBLs), or an appropriate framework for managing significant and rapid changes in their electricity demand.

IBLs include data centres, hydrogen electrolysers and other facilities driven by power electronics. Their demand can change rapidly, while data centres can also scale more quickly than traditional electricity loads because of their modular design.

AEMO forecasts data centre electricity consumption will increase from around 5TWh currently to approximately 34TWh over the next decade, lifting its share of National Electricity Market (NEM) operational demand from around 3 percent to 13 percent.

The AEMC is seeking feedback on two main areas of reform: a registration framework for large IBLs, and additional technical access standards covering communications, telemetry, remote monitoring and control, and the management of changes in active power demand.

On registration, the commission is considering adapting the existing NEM registration framework rather than creating a permanent new Registered Participant category specifically for large IBL operators. Registration could provide a mechanism for requiring data centres to supply information to AEMO, including through the Projected Assessment of System Adequacy (PASA) framework, and provide greater clarity around the application of operational directions.

The AEMC is seeking views on whether the 30MW threshold for large IBLs **established in its access standards rule finalised on 12 November** would be appropriate for registration, or whether a different threshold should apply. It is also considering whether requirements should cover existing facilities as well as new connections.

The consultation examines whether large IBLs should eventually participate as Voluntarily Scheduled Resources (VSRs) or scheduled loads. The AEMC says mandatory scheduled participation should not be imposed at this stage, given the diversity of operating models and the potential costs or constraints for facilities providing critical computing services. However, it considers the VSR framework could provide a stronger pathway for integrating flexible large loads into the market once implemented.

As the VSR framework has not yet commenced, the commission is also seeking feedback on interim arrangements. One option would be a temporary Registered Participant category for large IBL operators, allowing AEMO to issue directions directly to facility operators rather than through their existing Registered Participant, which is typically their electricity retailer.

### Further technical requirements

The second area of reform is around additional technical requirements intended to give AEMO and network service providers greater real-time visibility and control over large loads.

For communications and monitoring, the AEMC is consulting on a minimum access standard requiring large IBLs to provide real-time SCADA telemetry to AEMO, including active power and, for transmission-connected facilities, reactive power. A more comprehensive automatic standard would also provide two-way communications and remote-control capabilities, including over active-power limits and ramp rates. A negotiated standard between the two levels could be available where appropriate.

The commission is also consulting on a minimum limit for the rate at which large IBLs can change their active power demand: ±40MW per minute for the mainland NEM and ±10MW per minute in Tasmania. Faster rates could be negotiated where operators can demonstrate that their proposed demand changes can be accommodated without adversely affecting power system security.

The AEMC says these figures are initial proposals for consultation and will require further consideration of local and system-wide impacts, including the potential for multiple facilities to change demand at the same time. It also notes that workload management, power capping, rack-level controls and energy storage could help data centres manage their demand profiles.

The consultation builds on the AEMC’s final rule on NEM access standards, published on the same day, which established a 30MW definition for large IBLs and introduced new disturbance ride-through and instability-monitoring requirements. The new consultation would extend that framework beyond connection-stage technical requirements to address the ongoing operational visibility and management of large loads.

The rule change is part of a wider programme involving the AEMC, AEMO and Australian Energy Regulator, covering data centre energy contracting obligations, network augmentation costs, connection processes and operational visibility. Submissions on the consultation paper are due by 17 December 2026. The AEMC intends to publish a draft determination on 1 April 2027, subject to the complexity and materiality of issues raised by stakeholders.

stories.title: Swiftdata, owner of Nvidia-linked Megaspeed, lists address occupied by interior design firm
stories.summary: The co-founder of the ID firm said he has been operating there for more than four years
stories.title_zh: 与Nvidia关联的Megaspeed所有者Swiftdata登记的地址为室内设计公司所用
stories.content:
The co-founder of the ID firm said he has been operating there for more than four years

\[SINGAPORE\] A little-known Singapore company that owns Megaspeed International, the firm at the centre of US investigations into the possible diversion of advanced Nvidia chips to China, has a registered business address that an interior design firm says it has occupied for over four years.

Swiftdata, the parent company of Megaspeed – which saw a seemingly meteoric rise to become a massive buyer of Nvidia chips – did not appear to be occupying the unit at an integrated business hub when *The Straits Times* visited on Nov 11.

ST was unable to get in touch with Swiftdata.

The company, incorporated in 2023, is the sole shareholder in Megaspeed, owning all of its 10 million shares, according to Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority (ACRA) records.

The sole director of the company is Tan Yong Pong, who is also the sole director of Megaspeed, while Khloe Ng Wei Shi is listed as the corporate secretary for both firms.

ACRA records show that Ng is also the company secretary of the interior design firm and a holding company using the same Midview City address.

Swiftdata changed its registered address from an office building in Jurong East to Midview City in April.

No one answered when *The Straits Times* rang the doorbell of the unit, which had the greeting “hello” emblazoned at its entrance, alongside a shoe rack with four pairs of slippers.

Tenants in the building told ST the unit is occupied by an interior design firm.

When contacted, the co-founder of the firm said he leased the space directly from Midview City, and has been operating there for more than four years.

“I do not know Swiftdata, Megaspeed or any of their affiliates,” he said.

He said his firm is the “sole occupier of the address, someone somewhere must have used our address as a virtual address without our knowledge”.

Tenants on the same floor also said they had not encountered anyone associated with Swiftdata.

Asked about Swiftdata’s tenancy, Philip Chang, complex manager for Midview City, said he was “unable to provide any information due to PDPA regulations”.

The PDPA, or Personal Data Protection Act, governs the collection, use, disclosure and care of personal data in Singapore.

Megaspeed, which describes itself as a specialised cloud provider, is being probed in Singapore and the US. The US authorities began investigating Megaspeed over suspicions that it breached US chip export restrictions in late 2024.

Singapore police confirmed in October 2025 that they were investigating Megaspeed over “suspected breaches of our domestic laws”.

The firm returned to the spotlight in late October when news broke that the US was concerned about Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang’s close ties to Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive.

On Nov 8, Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with her.

Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was the director and managing director of Megaspeed from March to November 2023.

Previously known as 7Road International, Megaspeed’s ownership was transferred to Huang Le Limited when it was renamed in March 2023.

The firm became wholly-owned by the newly incorporated Swiftdata in November that year.

According to Bloomberg, Megaspeed, through its affiliates, imported at least US$4.6 billion (S$5.9 billion) worth of Nvidia hardware since its founding in 2023 to November 2025.

The news agency later reported that the “once-obscure spinoff of a Chinese gaming enterprise has evolved into the single largest South-east Asian buyer of Nvidia chips”.

According to ACRA records, Megaspeed’s total assets surged from US$32.9 million in 2023 to almost US$3 billion in 2024, in an almost 90-fold increase.

Its revenue rose from almost zero in 2023 to US$294.3 million in 2024, and its total liabilities jumped from US$22.9 million to almost US$3 billion over the same period.

Megaspeed has received unqualified audit opinions in recent years, which is the most favourable conclusion an auditor can issue after reviewing a company’s financial statements. It has not publicly disclosed its financial statements for 2025.

The company’s primary business activity is listed on ACRA as hosting services by non-data centres as a cloud service provider, while its secondary business activity is data analytics, processing, hosting and related activities.

It describes itself on its website as an Nvidia Cloud Partner and “a core business partner of Nvidia’s computing power cloud business in the Asia-Pacific region”.

Jensen Huang said in an interview on Oct 29 that Nvidia’s dealings with Megaspeed were “normal and not unusual”.

He added that Nvidia had checked to ensure that Megaspeed did not illegally send its artificial intelligence processors to China.

Nvidia, Alice Huang and Megaspeed did not respond to requests for comment. Media personnel have been denied access to Megaspeed’s registered address in Collyer Quay.

The whereabouts of Tan, the Singaporean and sole director of Swiftdata and Megaspeed, remain unclear.

When ST visited Tan’s registered residential address in the east of Singapore in October 2025, a family member said he no longer lived there and was believed to be in China.

Contacted again on Nov 10, the family member declined to say whether there had been any contact with Tan since ST’s previous visit, and directed ST’s queries to Megaspeed.

ST has approached ACRA on whether it has been in contact with Tan.

Under the Companies Act, local businesses must have a registered office in Singapore from incorporation that is able to receive communications and notices.

A requirement for the registered office to be open to the public for at least three hours on each business day was removed on Oct 20. THE STRAITS TIMES

stories.title: Data centre boom to require thousands of Australian tradespeople – Oxford Economics
stories.summary: Oxford Economics research projects that Australia's data center construction boom will require approximately 5,200 electricians, 4,200 plumbers and pipe fitters, and 2,600 mechanical and HVAC technicians annually from 2026 through 2030. The demand surge compounds existing pressures on Australia's skilled trades workforce from broader infrastructure and energy transition projects.
stories.why_it_matters: The projected labor shortfall threatens construction timelines and cost containment for data center developers, potentially delaying cloud and AI capacity deployment timelines by 12-24 months in a market already experiencing supply constraints. Wage inflation in specialized trades will cascade through project economics, favoring capital-rich hyperscale operators capable of premium labor recruitment over smaller colocation providers and enterprise self-builds, while intensifying political pressure for accelerated vocational training and skilled immigration pathway expansion.
stories.title_zh: 数据中心繁荣将需要数千名澳大利亚技术工人——Oxford Economics
stories.summary_zh: Oxford Economics研究预测，澳大利亚的数据中心建设热潮将在2026年至2030年期间每年需要约5,200名电工、4,200名管道工和管工，以及2,600名机械和HVAC技术人员。需求激增加剧了澳大利亚技术工人队伍来自更广泛基础设施和能源转型项目的现有压力。
stories.why_zh: 预计的劳动力短缺威胁数据中心开发商的建设时间表和成本控制，可能在已经经历供应约束的市场中将云和AI容量部署时间表延迟12-24个月。专业行业的工资通胀将贯穿项目经济学，有利于能够进行溢价劳动力招聘的资本雄厚的hyperscale运营商，而非较小的colocation提供商和企业自建，同时加剧对加速职业培训和扩大技术移民途径的政治压力。
stories.content:
Australia’s data centre construction pipeline could require an average of 5,200 full-time equivalent electricians, 4,200 plumbers and pipe fitters, and 2,600 mechanical and HVAC technicians each year between 2026 and 2030, adding to competition for skilled workers across an already stretched infrastructure sector.

The report warns that competition for specialised labour could push up wages and contractor costs, while increasing the risk of delays across data centre, energy, defence, hospital and other infrastructure projects.

The figures come from a new Oxford Economics briefing, Data centres boost demand for trades, which forecasts direct employment in Australia’s data centre industry will peak at approximately 38,400 workers in 2030. Around 36,000 of those jobs will be in construction and project delivery, compared with just 2,400 in the operation of completed facilities.

The report, authored by Oxford Economics economist Oscar Guth, estimates that data centre projects will account for around 22 percent of electrician demand across major projects nationally over the five-year period. They will represent approximately 40 percent of demand for plumbers and pipe fitters, and 38 percent for mechanical and HVAC technicians.

Oxford Economics expects non-IT work, which includes site infrastructure, shell construction, electrical and mechanical systems, fit-out and refurbishment, to rise eightfold from AU$4bn in 2024 to AU$32.4bn in 2030. At its peak, this will be equivalent to around 13 percent of all non-residential building and engineering construction undertaken in Australia.

The construction pipeline is expected to grow alongside other major infrastructure investment. Oxford Economics forecasts spending on major infrastructure projects, including data centres, will rise from approximately AU$106 billion in 2026 to AU$144bn in 2030. Within that, major energy-project construction spending is expected to increase from around AU$28bn to AU$45bn, reflecting both the transition to renewable energy and the demand for reliable power from data centres.

The additional demand comes as the infrastructure workforce is already experiencing significant shortages. Citing Infrastructure Australia estimates, Oxford Economics said the sector had a workforce of around 204,000 people in 2025 but faced a shortfall of approximately 141,000 workers. Job-advertising data shows pressure continuing to mount: since September 2025, ad postings have risen by 16 percent for electrical and telecommunications tradespeople, 10 percent for engineers and 5 percent for ICT technicians.

### Construction jobs spread beyond Sydney and Melbourne

The report also forecasts a significant geographic shift in data centre construction employment as development moves beyond Australia’s traditional Sydney and Melbourne markets.

Those two cities account for 87 percent of the sector’s construction workforce in 2026, but their share is expected to fall to 54 percent by 2030. Regional construction employment is forecast to increase from around 300 workers in 2026 to more than 10,000 in 2030, lifting the regional share from approximately 3 percent to 29 percent.

Oxford Economics said AI-focused data centres have different requirements from conventional facilities designed for data storage and retrieval. Their higher energy requirements and different specifications, alongside lower latency requirements, could make regional locations with abundant land and fewer approval constraints more attractive.

The investment is also expected to generate substantial indirect employment through domestic suppliers and additional household spending. Assuming the activity does not displace workers and resources from elsewhere in the economy, Oxford Economics estimates the industry could support a further 84,000 jobs indirectly through supply chains and 96,000 induced jobs through household spending in 2030.

However, the report cautions that existing supply constraints will limit the extent to which these potential employment gains can be realised, as competition for labour and other resources displaces activity elsewhere.

The outlook for ongoing operational employment is more modest. Much of the work involved in running data centre computing infrastructure is carried out off-site by hyperscale customers using existing software and global engineering teams. Australian neocloud providers could create additional local roles in cluster engineering, platform operations and customer support.

### Data centre boom compared with mining investment

A separate Oxford Economics briefing, Data centres and mining – a tale of two trade stories, examines whether Australia’s data centre investment boom can deliver the same economic benefits as the mining investment surge of the 2000s and early 2010s.

The report, authored by economist Harry McAuley, argues that although mining investment was larger in scale, a much larger proportion of data centre spending will flow overseas through imported equipment. At its peak, mining investment reached almost AU$130bn a year and accounted for roughly 9 percent of GDP.

Oxford Economics estimates that investment in data centre facilities and the high-specification equipment installed within them could exceed AU$240bn over the five years to 2030. It forecasts the value of data centre investment, including IT equipment, will grow from around AU$20bn in 2026 to more than AU$60bn in 2030.

However, up to three-quarters of the total investment value is expected to be allocated to imported goods, compared with an estimated peak of 45 percent during the mining investment boom.

IT equipment, including GPUs, CPUs, networking infrastructure and storage systems, is expected to account for around half of data centre investment through to 2030 and is almost entirely imported. In some AI-focused hyperscale projects, IT equipment could represent more than two-thirds of total investment. Australia currently has no advanced processor manufacturing capacity and is entirely reliant on imports for the most valuable segment of the data centre value chain.

Oxford Economics forecasts data centre-related imports will peak at just under AU$45bn in 2030, with more than two-thirds allocated to IT equipment. The report notes that servers, routers, storage and processing units accounted for almost half of data centre-related imports by value in the March 2026 quarter, with data processing units, memories and circuits representing 69 percent of those IT imports.

By comparison, during the mining boom, specialised equipment accounted for around 20 percent of industry capital expenditure, while Australian manufacturers and workers supplied much of the labour and materials for buildings and infrastructure.

The difference has implications for the domestic economic benefits of the current investment cycle. While mining exports subsequently repaid the import bill several times over and provided sustained support for Australia’s terms of trade and currency, the long-term export contribution of data centres remains less certain.

McAuley cites NextDC estimates that application, education and compute exports could generate AU$11bn over the five years to 2030. However, Oxford Economics argues this is a relatively small contribution compared with the value of imported components required to develop the infrastructure. Data processing unit imports alone totalled AU$5.2bn in the March 2026 quarter.

Instead, data centre operators and the federal government are banking on productivity gains and the adoption of AI across industries beyond the technology sector to make the broader economic case. The NextDC report estimates these gains could total AU$112bn over the same period, lifting GDP by 4 percent and average wages by 7 percent.

The Oxford Economics briefing also highlights the shorter replacement cycle for data centre equipment compared with mining infrastructure. GPUs and accelerators used for advanced computing are estimated to have a lifespan of four to six years, and in some cases may become obsolete sooner. By contrast, major mining assets such as processing plants and power infrastructure can last up to 30 years, while bulk transportation infrastructure can last up to 40 years.

This means data centre investment could generate repeated waves of equipment imports as operators upgrade their IT infrastructure, rather than a single initial investment cycle.

stories.title: AirTrunk targets 610MW of new renewable generation in NSW
stories.summary: AirTrunk has secured exclusive development rights for over 600 megawatts of renewable generation paired with more than 800 megawatt-hours of battery storage in New South Wales, specifically to support its proposed Kurri Kurri data center campus. The Hunter region projects include a 260-megawatt solar installation as part of a broader strategy to match data center load growth with dedicated clean energy supply.
stories.why_it_matters: The 800MWh battery storage component addresses intermittency challenges that have previously limited renewable-powered data center claims, enabling genuine 24/7 carbon-free operations rather than annualized matching. AirTrunk's vertical integration into generation development establishes a template that may become standard for large-scale Australian data center projects, though it raises questions about grid independence versus system contribution and whether such arrangements accelerate or delay broader national energy transition by concentrating renewable investment behind corporate offtake agreements.

stories.content:
AirTrunk and European Energy Australia have signed an exclusivity agreement to progress more than 600MW of renewable generation and over 800MWh of battery storage in New South Wales, as the data centre operator looks to support its growing electricity requirements, including its proposed Kurri Kurri campus.

The proposed Hunter region developments comprise a 260MW solar project, an 800MWh-plus battery energy storage system and a wind project of up to 350MW. Together, the projects could add 610MW of new renewable generation alongside the battery storage capacity to the NSW electricity system.

The companies are also discussing a potential long-term power purchase agreement (PPA) to support AirTrunk’s NSW energy requirements. However, the agreement remains under discussion, with the projects subject to further development, approvals, technical assessments and final grid connection arrangements.

European Energy plans to connect the projects to Ausgrid’s upgraded 132kV network in the Hunter-Central Coast Renewable Energy Zone. Solar and battery operations are targeted for 2030, with the wind project expected to begin operating in 2032.

The partnership builds on the companies’ work at the 31MW Mulwala Solar Farm in southern NSW, which officially opened this week and is now supplying renewable electricity to the state’s grid.

### Power for Kurri Kurri

The proposed renewable projects are intended to support AirTrunk’s wider NSW energy requirements, including its proposed data centre at Loxford, near Kurri Kurri, on the former Hydro Aluminium smelter site.

The proposed campus has a total power consumption of 550.5MW, according to its NSW planning application, and would reuse an established industrial site in the Hunter region. Its planning application was on public exhibition until 11 November.

AirTrunk says the Hunter projects are an important step towards supporting the campus, but acknowledges further renewable generation and firming capacity will be required to meet its wider NSW demand.

“We understand the community wants to know how Kurri Kurri’s electricity needs will be supported. Our focus is on bringing new renewable generation forward and securing renewable electricity through long-term supply arrangements,” said Sabooh Whitelaw, AirTrunk’s AVP Energy.

AirTrunk founder and CEO Robin Khuda (*above*) said “Digital growth must bring new energy with it. The Australian government’s expectations and NSW’s guidelines set a high bar for the industry. This partnership is an important step towards delivering on that commitment.”

The Australian government expects new data centres to support additional clean energy generation and storage, while NSW’s data centre guidelines similarly call on operators to fund the additional energy supply and infrastructure required by their developments.

AirTrunk says it is on track to match 100 percent of its electricity consumption with renewable energy by 2030. Around 73 percent of its electricity use across its portfolio was matched with renewable energy in FY26.

European Energy Australia managing director Catriona McLeod said “Partnerships like this allow us to bring more renewables online and add more energy to the grid.”

stories.title: Singapore cannot afford to let bad actors trade on its trust
stories.summary: The Nvidia scandal exposes the recurring threat of ‘reputation-laundering’
stories.title_zh: 新加坡不能让不良行为者利用其信任进行交易
stories.content:
The Nvidia scandal exposes the recurring threat of ‘reputation-laundering’

#### Annabeth Leow

\[SINGAPORE\] The news of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s extramarital liaison with an alleged Chinese spy should perturb Singaporeans – if nothing else, because the woman in question reportedly entered his circles as the executive of a Singapore-registered data-centre company.

Even before the news of the affair broke, that company, Megaspeed, came to attention in late 2025 as the subject of separate probes – both in the US and Singapore – around alleged contravention of US curbs on the sale of Nvidia chips to China.

Blending adultery, espionage and international trade conflict, the ongoing scandal is another troubling instance of a Singaporean connection to cases of transnational intrigue.

Unfortunately, the Republic’s pro-business landscape, and crucially, a reputation for zero tolerance of corruption, have created a phenomenon that some dub “Singapore-washing”.

## Destination: Singapore

The term, referring to the use of a Singapore base to downplay affiliations to mainland China and circumvent scrutiny from unfriendly regulators, was popularised a few years back, amid worsening trade and geopolitical tensions between Washington and Beijing.

The practice of shopping for a convenient jurisdiction in which to do business is not inherently wrong, and the vast majority of companies relocating to Singapore have been operating above board.

Still, the idea that setting up shop in Singapore lends a veneer of legitimacy to questionable corporate activities has been around for a long time.

Remember “S-chips”? In the 2010s, these Singapore-listed, China-based corporate equities picked up the stench of what *The Business Times* senior correspondent Jude Chan vividly recounts as “‘missing’ cash piles, phantom factories and the sudden disappearances of CEOs”.

Dodgy players were able to leverage a Singapore bourse membership to win the trust of the retail investors who ultimately ended up burnt by dubious stocks.

Nonetheless, potential Singapore-washing is not the province of companies from any single nation.

For instance, while the large agricultural plantations that have been fingered for potential culpability in episodes of regional smoke pollution are located in Malaysia and Indonesia, many of their operators are registered and headquartered in Singapore, and even listed on the Singapore Exchange.

## Cleaning house

Still, even if they are calculatedly capitalising on a Singaporean association, legitimate businesses, including the family-owned plantation conglomerates with complex transnational supply chains, naturally have an incentive to comply with the law.

The waters get muddier when malicious actors – such as alleged smugglers, sanctions evaders, money launderers or even spies – are thrown into the mix.

Companies elect to set up shop in Singapore for an array of reasons, many of them valid. The ease of incorporating a business is often cited as a strong point. But bad apples, both foreign and domestic, have long taken advantage of this ease for their own nefarious ends.

The Republic must continue to strenuously guard against “reputation-laundering” efforts, especially when these activities may carry serious economic and geopolitical implications, and negatively affect legitimate companies conducting business by the book.

That efforts at Singapore-washing have persisted over the decades indicates the immense challenge of surveillance and enforcement. Still, the authorities must be both vigilant and proactive in closing loopholes and prosecuting malefactors.

English playwright and poet William Shakespeare famously wrote in *Othello* that “he that filches from me my good name… makes me poor indeed”.

Singapore has long traded on its reputation. Policymakers cannot tolerate any action that would tarnish the value of this vaunted and irreplaceable asset.

stories.title: Sea's cloud business is the ideal defence for Shopee's market share
stories.summary: Sea aims to use its know-how in developing AI capacity to show others how it’s done – and make money too
stories.title_zh: Sea的cloud业务是Shopee市场份额的理想防御
stories.content:
Sea aims to use its know-how in developing AI capacity to show others how it’s done – and make money too

\[SINGAPORE\] Amid intense competition on the e-commerce front, Sea’s cloud business could be just the thing to help it fend off its rivals.

Sea’s recent Q3 2026 earnings revealed that its e-commerce arm Shopee, had its most profitable quarter ever, with adjusted earnings before interest, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) rising 44.5 per cent to US$269 million from US$186.1 million in the year before.

The figure was also higher than the second quarter’s Ebitda of US$255.4 million.

Revenue for Q3 2026 grew 41.3 per cent to US$6.1 billion from US$4.3 billion in the corresponding period.

## Heat from rivals

These were strong results, but Shopee has felt the competition – particularly that from Bytedance’s TikTok Shop – nipping at its heels in the last three years.

Recently, TikTok Shop launched a separate app in South-east Asia, which attests to the e-commerce business’ ability to stand on its own, rather than just being a tab on the TikTok app.

Hiving off TikTok Shop enables it to operate outside the constraints of the TikTok app; the e-commerce team can now shape customers’ behaviour, consultancy Momentum Works said in a note.

Other newer competitors are also jockeying for position. Chinese e-commerce company Pinduoduo is ramping up its efforts in Singapore; both its platforms Temu and Pinduoduo are mounting heavy advertising and marketing campaigns.

Then there is also Mercado Libre, the e-commerce incumbent in Brazil, which competes with Shopee on the South American continent.

There are barriers to entry in starting and running a successful e-commerce business, but they are not insurmountable. The players in this arena know that low prices and free shipping can draw customers, and that merchants can be enticed on board with lower fees and better reach.

## Sea chief explains the pivot

Against this backdrop, CEO Forrest Li’s announced in a note to Sea employees on Oct 20 that the company was entering the cloud business. The news was less of a surprise and more like a sustainable way to build a new revenue stream.

He disclosed more details and the management’s thinking on the subject in the recent Q3 2026 earnings call. He said that, rather than looking to build artificial intelligence infrastructure with data centres, the focus would instead be on helping enterprises adopt AI.

Sea intends to take its own lessons from developing AI capabilities and show others how it can be done, in areas where it has had success, such as with fraud detection, customer services and content generation. The aim is to turn this cost centre into a revenue stream.

“By serving external customers on top of that existing base, we can spread our fixed costs among more users and earn attractive incremental returns on capital,” said Li.

Sea is not closing itself off from potentially building and running data centres either; he said that if there is customer demand and attractive returns, Sea would pursue such opportunities.

The timing of such a business could not be any better, as enterprises are seeking to squeeze more value out of their AI tokens – now getting cheaper – after a spell of “token maxxing”.

Li said: “The real opportunity is to build a significant business around the long-term decline in token prices, and help organisations drive much broader AI adoption.”

Sea’s route into the cloud business is not entirely a fresh one: US e-commerce giant Amazon spun off its cloud business, Amazon Web Services (AWS), initially building it to solve its own issues, and then pivoting to running it for external customers.

It has worked well for Amazon. AWS now contributes to the bulk of Amazon’s net income, making US$17.7 billion of the giant’s US$20.7 billion net income for Q3 2026.

For Shopee, building this new cloud business even while it is the forerunner in South-east Asia’s e-commerce market, could be the way to build up sufficient resources, to continue to defend its market share.

stories.content:
The US has not posted any additions to its Entity List since October 2025

\[WASHINGTON\] US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick stalled President Donald Trump’s crackdown on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia’s chips to China, Axios reported on Wednesday (Nov 11), citing high-level sources.

Trump on Thursday of last week authorised a crackdown on companies suspected of diverting the chips for the third time this year, Axios reported, adding that the Republican president consulted billionaire Elon Musk before giving the go-ahead.

But Axios reported that Lutnick has repeatedly stood in the way.

The White House and a spokesperson for Lutnick did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Lutnick met in the Situation Room last Thursday with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Axios said.

During the meeting, Bessent confronted Lutnick about resistance from his department to implementing export controls. Lutnick appeared to agree but said he needed to check with Trump, according to the Axios report.

Several US lawmakers have said in recent days they want the Trump administration to take a tougher stance on exporting US chips to China and have called on Congress to approve legislation toughening restrictions, following disclosures about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

Nvidia’s board launched an investigation after reports that Huang had a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who US intelligence officials believed was spying for Beijing.

In June, Reuters reported that the Trump administration had held off from adding China’s AI startup DeepSeek, memory chipmaker CXMT and more than 100 other companies flagged as national security risks to a trade blacklist.

The US has not posted any additions to its Entity List since October 2025, the longest stretch between new postings in more than a decade. REUTERS

stories.summary: AirTrunk and European Energy Australia have entered an exclusive arrangement to develop two renewable energy projects in New South Wales' Hunter region, representing a $1.5 billion clean power commitment. - **Hunter renewable projects could add more than 600 megawatts (MW) of new generation plus 800+ megawatt hours (MWh) of storage.**
- **Projects will support AirTrunk’s NSW energy needs, including its proposed Kurri Kurri site.**
- **Partnership builds on the newly opened Mulwala Solar Farm in New South Wales.**
- **AirTrunk on track to match all electricity use with renewables by 2030.**

Hyperscale data centre specialist AirTrunk and renewable energy developer, builder, owner and operator European Energy Australia have signed an exclusivity agreement to progress two renewable energy projects in the Hunter region in New South Wales, Australia.

The proposed projects include a 260 MW solar project, an 800+ MWh battery project and up to 350 MW wind project in the Hunter-Central Coast Renewable Energy Zone. Together, they could add more than a gigawatt of new renewables generation and storage to NSW’s electricity system.

The companies are progressing project development and discussing a potential long-term power purchase agreement to support AirTrunk’s NSW energy requirements, including its proposed Kurri Kurri data centre campus.

The projects are expected to begin operating between 2030 (solar and battery) and 2032 (wind), with European Energy planning to connect them to Ausgrid’s upgraded 132 kilovolt network in the Hunter-Central Coast Renewable Energy Zone. The connections will be subject to final connection arrangements, approvals and further technical assessments.

### AirTrunk meeting government expectations for new energy supply

The Australian Government expects new data centres to secure new and additional clean energy generation and/or storage to offset their demand, while managing energy use and contributing to a secure and stable electricity grid. The NSW Data Centre Guidelines similarly expect operators to fund the additional energy supply and infrastructure their projects require, without shifting net costs to households, businesses or communities.

AirTrunk is working with energy partners and networks to bring new supply forward alongside its growth. The proposed Hunter projects and discussions about a long-term power purchase agreement form part of that work. The projects and potential agreement remain subject to further development, approvals and final arrangements.

**Robin Khuda, Founder and CEO of AirTrunk, said:** “Digital growth must bring new energy with it. The Australian Government’s expectations and NSW’s guidelines set a high bar for the industry. This partnership is an important step towards delivering on that commitment.”

**Sabooh Whitelaw, AVP Energy at AirTrunk, said:** “We understand the community wants to know how Kurri Kurri’s electricity needs will be supported. Our focus is on bringing new renewable generation forward and securing renewable electricity through long-term supply arrangements.”

**Catriona McLeod, Managing Director, European Energy Australia said:** “It’s great to see AirTrunk and the tech sector embracing renewable energy – partnerships like this allow us to bring more renewables online and add more energy to the grid.”

The partnership builds on AirTrunk and European Energy Australia’s work at the 31 MW Mulwala Solar Farm, which officially opened this week and is now supplying renewable electricity to NSW’s grid. The companies will continue to explore further renewable energy opportunities.

### New Hunter renewables to support AirTrunk’s Kurri Kurri proposal

AirTrunk is proposing a data centre on the former Kurri Kurri smelter site at Loxford, reusing land with an established industrial history. The project would support jobs and economic opportunities in the Hunter and make use of existing infrastructure.

Over the past four months, AirTrunk has engaged with the local community through information sessions, project updates and a drop-in hub. AirTrunk will continue listening and sharing information as the proposal progresses through the planning process.

Whitelaw added, “The Hunter projects are an important step, but more renewable generation and firming will be needed to support Kurri Kurri and AirTrunk’s wider NSW needs. We’ll continue working with developers and energy partners to progress further projects across Australia”.

### AirTrunk is on track to match all electricity use with renewables by 2030

AirTrunk is committed to matching 100% of its electricity use with renewable energy by 2030 as part of its Net Zero 2030 target. In FY26, around 73% of its electricity use was matched with renewable energy across the portfolio. The company is working to increase that share by supporting new renewable generation and securing long-term supply as its operations grow.

stories.title: Greenfield versus Brownfield: How data center projects are evolving around the constraints
stories.summary: Data centers have evolved from single halls to campuses that span hundreds of acres. But as land and power become binding constraints, developers have been forced to rethink greenfield projects and consider adapting brownfields into something fit for purpose. Brendyn Lotz investigates how the binding constraints have forced developers to adapt their thinking around data […]
stories.title_zh: Greenfield与Brownfield：数据中心项目如何在约束条件下演进
stories.content:
*Data centers have evolved from single halls to campuses that span hundreds of acres. But as land and power become binding constraints, developers have been forced to rethink greenfield projects and consider adapting brownfields into something fit for purpose. Brendyn Lotz investigates how the binding constraints have forced developers to adapt their thinking around data center build outs.*

As Dickensien as it may be, it truly is the best and worst of times for data center operators. The spike in demand for AI infrastructure means that data centers are in demand at a level previously not seen before.

At the same time, the operating environment for data centers couldn’t be more abrasive. Lawmakers, pushed by constituents, are rewriting the rules mid buildout, pushing data center developers to invest more, guard, or outright refrain from using public resources and rely less on tax cuts and legislative mechanisms to push projects through the halls of councils.

The demand for AI compute power isn’t going away and developers hoping to capitalize on that demand must not only navigate the quagmire of public opinion, but also plan for the future.

This demand means that the type of facility being built is evolving. Traditional data centers were designed to operate with power draws up to 18kW per rack but AI workloads demand even more with NVIDIA’s Rubin Ultra platform demanding at least 600kW per rack with liquid cooling a requirement rather than an option. This evolution represents a fundamental shift in how data center buildouts are approached.

As data center operators scramble to house the AI workloads that are driving the sector forward, they face a foundational choice that will define the next decade of the industry. Do they build something entirely new on empty land, or adapt what already exists?

The greenfield and brownfield decision is no longer a routine real-estate question. It has become a strategic bet based on the scarcity of space, power, time, and money.

#### Tried and tested: The greenfield approach

Greenfield projects are, as the terminology implies, a fresh site. A developer will select a site with ample land capable of supporting their vision and build. These sites are devoid of infrastructure and as such, need connectivity, power and other utilities run to them which carries a cost.

This has been the defacto approach for developers for many years as it made sense to start from scratch and build out a site according to the required specifications. Site selection is not just about finding a space big enough to accommodate a data center, the site must also be safe and firms like Digital Realty assess various factors regarding a site including the potential for natural disasters, climate and other environmental hazards.

But as AI demand grows, the selection criteria for greenfield projects has become far more complex. Securing land with close proximity to power, water, and connectivity is a good start, but it’s just the start.

“When selecting new datacenter sites, we consider a range of criteria, including proximity to population centers, a broad, reliable, and stable power source, multiple high-capacity network connections, a large pool of qualified labor, and affordable and renewable energy. To enhance the availability, security, and performance of our cloud infrastructure, we also seek sites within a certain geographic radius of each other,” a spokesperson for Microsoft tells us regarding how the firm selects sites for its data center buildouts.

Of course, power availability is a going concern for all developers but so is grid availability. National grids from Mombasa to Mumbai were never designed to support multi-gigawatt AI data centers and so developers are waiting months for a connection to the grid. It’s not just about the power, even if a developer brings their own power, transmission infrastructure, substations, and distribution equipment must all be upgraded to support the generation.

According to analysis of the delays holding back buildouts by Hanwha Data Centers, operators are increasingly subject to studies conducted by utilities to judge how the interconnection request will affect existing infrastructure. One study can act as a catalyst, leading to other studies and so on and so forth. Before an operator knows it, they could be waiting years for one of these studies to be completed before a grid approval can be considered.

Even when those studies wrap up quickly, supply chains bogged down by a surge in demand make acquiring the requisite infrastructure far tougher than it has ever been. According to Wood Mackenzie, power transformer lead times have ballooned from a 50 week wait time in 2021 to as much as three years in 2026. That’s a three year delay that simply isn’t tenable in the current climate. And that’s not even mentioning the delays associated with grid connections which can span up to seven years in some parts of the US.

In recent months another consideration has become more prominent for all developers, the community surrounding the development.

Resistance from communities where data center proposals exist has seen multi-billion dollar projects canceled before ground has even been broken. State-wide moratoriums on new data centers are gaining momentum with New York state becoming the first to issue a ban on new AI data center buildouts in June. While less toothsome, even Texas has outlined new regulations for data centers hoping to put roots down in the Lone Star State.

These problems start to compound and eventually developers will retract as QTS Data Centers and Compass Datacenters did in Northern Virginia in July with the 2,100 acre Digital Gateway project that would have brought in over US$ 100 billion in spending in what could have been one of the largest technology corridors around the world.

As such, firms like Microsoft are now working closely with local utilities and permitting authorities to ensure that data centers are built to not only effectively service existing customers, but work with the surrounding communities as well.

#### A golden brown(field) opportunity

A brownfield site sees an existing commercial or industrial facility being converted into a data center. The benefit of this approach is that the initial costs can be far lower and there is far less pushback from community members as the data center is set to be located on land that is already part of urban sprawl.

“By accelerating speed to market, brownfield projects provide a competitive edge. This approach eliminates challenges associated with new data center builds such as grid interconnection delays, limited land availability, and asset monetization. AI deployment in existing data centers provides an easier growth path, not merely a workaround, giving operators a faster time to revenue,” explains Andrew Whitmore, Vice President of Sales at Motivair by Schneider Electric.

As attractive as a faster time to revenue maybe, brownfield projects come with their own unique challenges.

For example, the US Department of Energy announced in 2025 that it planned to use land it owns for colocation data centers. One of those sites is the Savannah River Site which, until 1988, was a production facility for plutonium and tritium destined for nuclear weapons. The Department of Energy’s Office of Environmental Management notes that a significant portion of its US$ 7.64 billion 2023 budget was earmarked for critical liquid waste cleanup at just three sites. While the data center project is separate from those cleanup operations, it is an integral part of preparing the site for a data center.

Environmental factors then are a key consideration for brownfield projects especially if a cleanup operation is required to alleviate potentially hazardous soil and groundwater conditions, adding further complexity that must be addressed.

Unlike a greenfield project, using an existing site is bound by what the land already features. This can be useful especially given the previously mentioned grid constraints, but the brownfield also dictates how much density can be supported. That is a key consideration, especially for those building AI data centers that need headroom and modern infrastructure to account for the constantly evolving state of compute hardware. Infrastructure can of course be modernized but there is a growing push from lawmakers to have developers modernize the infrastructure surrounding their projects and not only the infrastructure serving their facility. This capital expense can make a brownfield project less attractive, depending on the cost.

For many developers, brownfields aren’t suited for large scale AI data centers but rather AI inference facilities. AI inference doesn’t require an armada for GPUs to train a model and is instead focussed on putting an already trained model to use. While compute power is still a requirement the load shifts from an upper end of 1 GW to 100 MW. As such, many AI data centers in countries such as South Africa are geared toward inference rather than training.

“South Africa’s market is expected to be driven primarily by AI inference workloads rather than the multi-hundred-megawatt AI training campuses being developed in the United States, China, and the Middle East. AI inference deployments are smaller, more efficient, and avoid many of the complex grid connection challenges associated with hyperscale AI training facilities,” Bryce Allan, Teraco Head of Sustainability tells us.

Brownfield sites may be perfect for AI inference, especially in nascent markets trying to build a foothold in the sector and that have warehousing or other vacant industrial facilities accumulating rust.

#### The next evolution

One way to eliminate complexity, or at least a large chunk of it, is to reimagine data centers completely, and switch to modular construction.

A modular data center is an all-in-one solution that can be deployed and moved at a moment’s notice. These solutions contain compute power, optimized energy usage and modern cooling systems that can be interconnected to create a massive network of data centers suitable for high-density AI data centers or edge computing.

Modular data centers can accelerate time to revenue for operators and address demand for compute with fewer delays. Granted, a facility or shell is still needed as is power and connectivity, but a utility may be more inclined to grant 100 MW of power compared to 1 GW.

A modular approach may be the way forward for developers that are looking to deploy capacity quickly without the bottlenecks other projects subject to. This is especially useful for markets like Singapore where land is one of the biggest constraints holding back buildouts.

There are also floating data centers and orbital data centers which are increasingly becoming a part of the buildout conversation and cut out the land and grid connectivity problem entirely.

The unfortunate reality is that every data center buildout is bound to run into a problem, it is the nature of the beast. However, those same constraints are pushing developers to be more agile and thoughtful in regards to how these projects are managed from inception to completion.

Whether greenfield, brownfield or beyond, the best data center is the one that gets built and developers have a plethora of options they can choose from in order to turn a fledgling proposal into a mammoth data center.
