stories.title: Quantinuum upgrades quantum computer at Riken, partners with SoftBank for AI data center deployments
stories.summary: Quantinuum has upgraded its quantum computer at the Riken supercomputing center in Japan to its latest-generation system.
stories.title_zh: Quantinuum 升级 Riken 的量子计算机，并与 SoftBank 合作部署 AI 数据中心
stories.content:
Quantinuum has upgraded its quantum computer at the Riken supercomputing center in Japan to its latest-generation system.

The companies this week announced an expanded partnership that will see a “significant” upgrade to Quantinuum's Reimei quantum computer at Riken.

As well as working on potential quantum applications, the partners will work with Japanese universities and suppliers toward the development of a "Made with Japan" fault-tolerant quantum computer.

They will also collaborate with SoftBank Corp. to explore the connection of a quantum computer with AI data centers in Japan.

Quantinuum's quantum computer, Reimei, installed at Riken, has successfully completed its upgrade to the quantum firm’s 56-qubit System Model H2.

Reimei is operated as part of the JHPC-quantum project, funded by NEDO (New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization, an organization under Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry).

"Japan's quantum ambitions require advanced capabilities today and a sustained commitment to developing what comes next," said Dr. Rajeeb Hazra, Quantinuum CEO. "The upgrade to Reimei expands what we can explore with Riken across electronics, energy and life sciences. Together, we are building on this work to develop a fault-tolerant quantum computer with Japanese universities and suppliers, while exploring with SoftBank how these capabilities can become accessible to industry through Japan's AI data centers."

The two companies’ joint research and development toward a "Made with Japan" fault-tolerant quantum computer will involve Japanese universities and domestic components suppliers. The work effort will combine Quantinuum's quantum technology with domestic research and manufacturing expertise, drawing on experience from deploying and operating Reimei at Riken.

The original H1-version of Quantinuum’s Reimei system was deployed in February 2025, offering 20 qubits. The installation, at Riken in Wako, Saitama, was Quantinuum's first on-premise delivery of a system.

## Quantinuum & Riken work with SoftBank on quantum data centers

Under a separate agreement, Quantinuum, Riken, and SoftBank will explore how quantum computing can be connected directly with AI data centers in Japan.

The partners will assess infrastructure readiness and examine how connected systems could support commercial quantum-AI hybrid computing services.

"Japan has established a strong foundation for hybrid quantum-HPC computing through the NEDO-supported JHPC-quantum project," said Takenori Kobayashi, VP, head of product research & development division at SoftBank Corp. "Our responsibility is to turn these achievements into industrial value. Together with Riken and Quantinuum, we aim to advance a Quantum AI Datacenter that connects quantum computing with AI and HPC, making these capabilities accessible to businesses across Japan."

Quantinuum was founded in 2021 when Honeywell spun out its Quantum Solutions division and merged it with UK quantum computing startup Cambridge Quantum Computing. Honeywell owns a 54 percent stake in Quantinuum. IBM is also an investor.

Previously the preserve of custom white spaces at quantum computing company labs and supercomputing centers, quantum computers are increasingly being deployed in commercial data centers and linked to ‘classical’ GPU- and CPU-powered supercomputers.

stories.title: DXN signs Pacific CLS contract with unnamed Internet company
stories.summary: Australian modular data center company DXN has signed a contract to deliver a new cable landing station (CLS) module to a repeat customer.
stories.title_zh: DXN 与未具名互联网公司签署 Pacific CLS 合同
stories.content:
Australian modular data center company DXN has signed a contract to deliver a new cable landing station (CLS) module to a repeat customer.

The company announced this week that it has entered into a binding contract with an unnamed global Internet company for the design, supply, and commissioning of a modular CLS.

The contract is valued at approximately AU$4.8 million (approximately US$3.4 million),

The CLS is to be deployed to an unnamed Pacific region “site under US jurisdiction,” with delivery expected to the site in Q1 2028.

DXN said this is the fourth order with the same customer.

Shalini Lagrutta, managing director of DXN, said: "With this being the fourth contract with our global Internet Customer, we now have a deep relationship and understanding of the customer requirements and have been able to help standardize a solution fit for purpose for their global deployment, that is prefabricated, modular and standardized from start to finish. We look forward to delivering this project on schedule and to the highest quality standards, and to building on this relationship as our customer continues its global infrastructure expansion."

DXN has delivered more than 100 modular data centers to date. Customers include logistics firm DP World, AngloAmerican, gold miner Newcrest in New South Wales, Stanmore Coal, as well as Boeing, Covalent Lithium, Pilbara Minerals, satellite firm Globalstar, and Melbourne Airport.

The company has previously delivered cable landing station modules to Sub.co on the Cocos (Keeling) Islands for the Oman – Australia Cable and to the island of Palau for the Meta/Google-led Echo subsea cable. It was also the CLS provider for the East Micronesia Cable System (EMCS), and last year announced it was to deliver one to consulting firm APTelecom for an unnamed "international digital infrastructure project."

The firm is also delivering a CLS to the American Samoa Telecommunications Authority that will host the upcoming La Vasa subsea cable, a US$45 million subsea fiber-optic system connecting American Samoa with Fiji and French Polynesia, and will connect to Google’s upcoming Bulikula system.

stories.title: Rakuten, AST SpaceMobile to form official Japan D2D constellation; promise Edge compute in space
stories.summary: Rakuten and AST SpaceMobile have announced a joint venture to build a direct-to-device (D2D) communications network in Japan using low-Earth orbit (LEO) satellites.
stories.title_zh: Rakuten与AST SpaceMobile组建日本官方D2D星座；承诺太空Edge compute
stories.content:
Rakuten and AST SpaceMobile have announced a joint venture to build a direct-to-device (D2D) communications network in Japan using low-Earth orbit (LEO) satellites.

The firms won a tender from Japan’s Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications (MIC) to form Rakuten AST as part of the Japan Low Earth Orbit Satellite Communications Project (J-LEO). The joint venture is expected to receive around $1 billion from MIC to support deployment of a Japanese-flagged mid-band satellite constellation, with domestic operations due to begin in early 2029.

The non-terrestrial network (NTN) will see Rakuten leverage AST SpaceMobile's satellites to enable high-speed internet connectivity for smartphone users in the country. Rakuten AST also plans to work with the US satellite giant to provide the same services to AST SpaceMobile's global customers.

## AST SpaceMobile, Japan, and SpaceX: Rakuten the outlier

Rakuten’s relationship with AST dates back to 2020, when the firms signed a commercial agreement to develop connectivity compatible with Rakuten’s Japanese mobile network. The same year saw it join Vodafone as a lead investor in what was then known as AST & Science, bringing its total capital to $128 million.

Rakuten remains the sole major Japanese operator to work with AST, with KDDI, SoftBank, and NTT DoCoMo favoring SpaceX for their D2D efforts.

Rakuten Mobile will also work with AST SpaceMobile to advance the use of AI Edge computing in the stars, as well as developing AI-driven spectrum management technology. According to Rakuten, this research will explore their applications for faster data communications and industry-specific solutions like IoT to pitch to verticals including logistics, infrastructure monitoring, and construction.

At this year’s London edition of the Xcelerated Compute Show, David Anderson, chief product officer (CPO) of non-terrestrial infra player Ramon Space, told this title that IoT is a leading use case for space-based compute.

“Our cell phones today can actually start talking to satellites directly, so having that compute truly at the Edge is very advantageous, and that plants the business case and the seed to say there's demand today that has nothing to do with the power and regulatory constraints of terrestrial data centers,” Anderson said.

Anderson also claimed space-based Edge computing makes sense considering the amount of data that already exists not only from IoT connectivity, but also communications, radar, and D2D connections.

“People are trying to solve the communications bottleneck of how you get all this data down, and (Edge computing) is a great way to solve the communication bottleneck,” Anderson said.

stories.title: Liquid cooling is changing how we design and deploy the entire rack: Q&A with Matt McGuff, Jabil
stories.summary: The excitement surrounding liquid cooling continues to grow with the burgeoning demand for AI infrastructure across the world. With rack densities increasing and AI factories being planned across all major markets, we caught up with Matt McGuff, Senior Director of Technology Strategy and System Architecture, Intelligent Infrastructure division, Jabil, to take a deep dive into […]
stories.title_zh: 液体冷却正在改变我们设计和部署整个机架的方式：Jabil Matt McGuff 问答
stories.content:
The excitement surrounding liquid cooling continues to grow with the burgeoning demand for AI infrastructure across the world. With rack densities increasing and AI factories being planned across all major markets, we caught up with Matt McGuff, Senior Director of Technology Strategy and System Architecture, Intelligent Infrastructure division, Jabil, to take a deep dive into the future of liquid cooling.

##### Q-1) How have you seen liquid cooling technology evolve? Will it gradually phase out traditional cooling methods?

Liquid cooling has moved from a niche high-performance computing technology to a foundational requirement for AI infrastructure. Over the past several generations, xPU (GPU, CPU and custom accelerator) power has climbed from a few hundred watts to more than 1 kW, with next-gen designs enabling 5kW. Rack densities have risen from 10–20 kW to well over 100 kW in today’s AI racks, with roadmaps projecting several hundred kilowatts and potentially 1 MW.

At those densities, cooling can no longer be treated as a standalone subsystem. It must be designed alongside compute, networking, power, rack mechanics and the data center environment.

That said, we don’t expect liquid cooling to replace air cooling across the board. Even liquid-cooled racks reject some heat to air, and general-purpose compute will remain largely air-cooled for years. The reality is hybrid, with liquid becoming the default for AI compute.

##### Q-2) Given increasing rack densities, how is liquid cooling changing rack design, validation, deployment readiness, and operations?

*“Liquid cooling is not just changing how we cool a server. It is changing how we design, manufacture, test and deploy the entire rack.”*

Higher-density racks turn cooling from a component challenge into a system-level one. Effective design starts with the data center: how facility water is delivered, available flow rates, connection requirements, coolant type, and the location and specification of the CDU. At the rack level, the design must account for flow balancing, pressure drop, leak detection and how the system responds if a leak occurs.

Engineering labs and manufacturing lines must adapt too. They need facility water and equipment to fill, purge and service coolant loops. Testing covers pressure drop, leak detection, flow balancing across manifolds and coolant cleanliness, since microchannel cold plates are sensitive to particulates, followed by full-power thermal testing under real or simulated workloads. Manufacturers also need to plan how racks are shipped, filled or dry, and protected from shock and vibration in transit.

With liquid cooling, the risk moves upstream. Issues that might once have been fixed on site must be eliminated before the rack ships, and the facility’s cooling loop must be clean, commissioned and ready to receive it.

In operation, serviceability and visibility must be designed from the start. That means telemetry and leak detection integrated with facility monitoring, disciplined coolant management, and components that can be serviced without disrupting neighboring systems.

##### Q-3) In light of the growing pressure on cooling infrastructure, how are hyperscalers adopting integrated rack-level solutions?

Rack-scale procurement is not new for hyperscalers. What has changed is how interdependent the components inside the rack have become, and how quickly new capacity must come online.

Many hyperscalers own their rack and cooling designs, often building on open standards such as OCP. What they need from manufacturing partners is the ability to take those designs into volume production quickly, rather than a fixed off-the-shelf product. Custom silicon adds to this: each new accelerator brings its own rack configuration, with its own thermal and power requirements.

Hyperscalers also ramp capacity across several regions at once, so the same validated configuration must be built identically at every site. And while new liquid-ready facilities are under construction, many are using sidecar and liquid-to-air approaches to bring liquid cooling into existing halls.

##### Q-4) As rack-level integration becomes critical to AI infrastructure deployment, what are some of the challenges operators face in making this happen?

The biggest challenge is managing system complexity at speed and scale, while the technology keeps moving.

AI platforms now evolve roughly annually, so operators are building facilities today for racks two or three generations away, without knowing exactly what power and cooling those racks will require. Many are also retrofitting air-cooled halls that were never designed for heavy, liquid-cooled racks. Meanwhile, every week of delay leaves expensive compute idle, so time to capacity is critical.

These issues are interconnected. A change in cooling architecture affects power, mechanics and serviceability, and with standards still maturing, operators often must coordinate many suppliers and work out who is accountable when something goes wrong. Those expanding across several markets also need racks that perform and are serviced consistently everywhere. In Asia-Pacific, grid capacity, permitting and a shortage of experienced liquid-cooling technicians add further pressure.

That’s why integration matters. Pre-validated rack configurations, consistent manufacturing and traceability across regions, and a single accountable partner across cooling, power and mechanics help operators reduce risk and deploy faster.

##### Q-5) How important is it to validate power, thermal management, networking, and optics as a complete system?

It is critical. AI infrastructure is increasingly a system of systems, and components that pass individual testing don’t necessarily perform as expected once everything runs together.

The interactions are where problems hide. Power spikes from AI workloads stress both power delivery and cooling response at the same time. Changes in cooling design can push heat-sensitive optics out of their operating range. And a single xPU throttling because of uneven coolant flow can slow an entire training job across a cluster. Found on site, these issues mean delays, idle compute and costly rework.

Validation therefore needs to progress from component and subsystem testing to rack-level and, where applicable, cluster-level validation, so integration problems are found in a controlled engineering and manufacturing environment rather than on the customer’s data center floor. As co-packaged optics and liquid-cooled networking become more common, these interdependencies will only increase.

##### Q-6) How can infrastructure providers reduce deployment risks and accelerate time-to-capacity?

The biggest opportunity is to remove iterations, handoffs and surprises between design and deployment.

That starts with engaging early, co-designing with chip vendors and operators so systems are built for manufacturability and serviceability from day one rather than redesigned later. It continues with standardization: reference designs and rack platforms that carry across chip generations mean each deployment isn’t a fresh engineering project. And it means completing integration in the factory, so racks arrive as tested systems rather than parts to assemble on site.

The facility side matters just as much. Prefabricated power and cooling infrastructure can be built and tested in parallel with site construction rather than after it. Securing long-lead components early, and building validated configurations identically everywhere, removes common causes of delay.

##### Q-7) What trends and innovations do you foresee with respect to liquid cooling adoption in 2027?

2027 looks like an inflection point. Five trends stand out:

1. **Rack power will step up sharply.** Announced industry roadmaps point to racks of several hundred kilowatts and 800 VDC power distribution in 2027. At those levels, power and cooling can no longer be designed separately.
2. **Liquid cooling will extend across the rack.** Beyond xPUs, power components, busbars, memory and networking will increasingly be liquid-cooled, and co-packaged optics will add to that.
3. **Warmer coolant and new cold plate approaches will gain ground.** Designs running at coolant temperatures of 45°C or higher reduce or remove the need for chillers, a significant advantage in hot, humid climates across Asia-Pacific. For the highest-power chips, direct-to-die and two-phase cooling will move closer to mainstream adoption.
4. **Adoption will broaden beyond hyperscalers.** Neoclouds, sovereign AI programs, colocation providers and enterprises will adopt liquid cooling at scale, many through sidecar and retrofit approaches that bring liquid into existing facilities. Greater standardization of interfaces will make that easier.
5. **Manufacturing and diagnostics will get smarter.** Digital traceability, AI-assisted diagnostics and real-time process data will support the manufacturing of complex rack-scale systems, and will increasingly follow the rack into operation, helping operators diagnose and resolve issues faster.

\* Jabil is a global provider of engineering, supply chain, and manufacturing solutions. Founded in 1966 in Detroit, Michigan, Jabil established its cloud and data center business in 2014.

stories.title: Five reasons why Nvidia matters – and what's now at stake
stories.summary: Nvidia's central role in AI infrastructure has made it a dominant position in major investment fund portfolios, while questions about leadership succession for CEO Jensen Huang have gained prominence. The company's market influence extends beyond semiconductor supply to encompass data center design standards, AI software ecosystems, and energy consumption patterns for digital infrastructure globally.

stories.content:
Major funds’ portfolios may be impacted while there are leadership questions to answer if Jensen Huang leaves

\[SAN FRANCISCO\] It’s not often that a revelation about a relationship erases a trillion dollars of value from the stock market. But that’s what’s happened in the wake of media reports that a woman suspected of being an asset for Chinese intelligence had grown close to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who acknowledged having an extramarital affair.

The wipeout speaks both to the chipmaker’s sheer size – at around US$4 trillion, Nvidia’s market capitalisation is comparable to the national economic output of Japan, the UK or India – and to the pivotal role of its leather-jacketed, celebrity CEO.

It was Huang’s decision to pivot Nvidia’s focus from graphics chips for gaming to the artificial intelligence “accelerators” that have made it one the world’s biggest companies by market value, and his globe-trotting lobbying has helped to maintain its dominant position.

Hence the sharp sell-off of Nvidia’s shares when the espionage scandal raised questions about his future at the company. A spokesperson for China’s government called the “so-called Chinese spy allegation” unsubstantiated.

Here’s why the stakes are so high.

## Market titan

On Nov 30, 2022, a then-little-known company called OpenAI released a chatbot called ChatGPT, triggering an explosion in demand for a type of computing chip that Nvidia was uniquely well-placed to provide. After that, Nvidia’s share price rose fourteen-fold to a peak on Oct 6.

The company witnessed soaring demand from data-centre customers, including Alphabet, Amazon.com and Microsoft. In mid-2024, it overtook all three by market capitalisation for the first time. In 2025, Nvidia became the first company to surpass both US$4 trillion and US$5 trillion in market value.

By early October, it was closing in on the US$6 trillion mark. Since then, it’s fallen behind Apple as the world’s biggest company. Investors have become increasingly skittish over frothy AI stock valuations and an industry borrowing spree.

And the Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections has cast doubt over the sustainability of an AI data centre construction boom. By Nov 10, the revelations about Huang’s affair had pushed Nvidia’s valuation to a level almost on par with the No 3 company, Microsoft.

## Chip supremacy

Nvidia today accounts for an overwhelming share of sales of the advanced chips that process AI tasks. Its dominance partly reflects a substantial head start: Years before AI really took off, the company was investing in ways to use its graphics processing units for uses beyond gaming.

It has maintained that lead by rolling out new designs every year. Its size and purchasing power have kept it ahead of the game, making it harder for smaller rivals to keep up.

Now is a particularly bad time for the company to be risking a leadership crisis. Nvidia’s rivals, and even some of its customers, are working hard to develop competitive AI chips. A raft of startups are raising billions of dollars from investors keen to back the next breakthrough.

Competition is also intensifying in China, where the company is prevented by US export controls from selling its most advanced products. Companies such as Huawei Technologies – blacklisted in the US – are making rapid strides in developing home-grown AI chips, Nvidia has said.

## AI finance linchpin

Since 2024, Nvidia has become not just a supplier to the AI industry but also one of its key financial backers. It has invested heavily in leading AI platform developers including OpenAI, Elon Musk’s SpaceX and France’s Mistral, as well as companies building AI data centres.

It’s a symbiotic relationship: Nvidia helps to finance the expansion of AI infrastructure, stoking demand for Nvidia’s chips.

## Portfolio dominance

Until mid-2020 Nvidia’s market capitalisation represented less than 1 per cent of the total value of all the companies tracked in the S&P 500 index, the standard benchmark for the US stock market.

For much of the past two years, Nvidia’s share hovered around 8 per cent, the largest slice of any company. In the wake of the news about Huang’s relationship with the suspected spy, it fell below 7 per cent and lower than Apple’s share.

Because of the company’s weight, its health can significantly affect the overall value of the S&P 500, to which enormous amounts of money are tied.

Some US$20 trillion in assets is either indexed or benchmarked to it, according to S&P Global. These are held largely through retirement funds, mutual funds and exchange-traded funds.

## Key-man risk

Huang is known for his exacting management style, even in an industry full of domineering CEOs who obsess over details. Every major decision flows through him, and he weighs in on even the most minute aspects of the business.

Huang has about 60 people reporting to him directly, far more than the average tech leader. They send him e-mails with “top five things” that he reads and responds to at all hours.

The spy scandal has underscored Nvidia’s “key-man” risk: Its 63-year-old CEO is seen as inseparable from the company’s success.

The board wants to keep Huang as CEO if possible, according to an employee who asked not to be identified, but an independent committee is investigating his actions.

Huang’s potential exit would put Nvidia in an unusually vulnerable position for a company of its size: There’s no one designated to replace him. BLOOMBERG

stories.content:
Criteria to qualify for transition financing updated for energy, maritime, iron and steel sectors as well

\[SINGAPORE\] Changes to energy-efficiency metrics of data centres are among some of the updates to the second edition of Singapore’s sustainable finance taxonomy.

In addition, the criteria for economic activities that qualify for sustainable or transition financing in the energy, maritime, and iron and steel sectors were also revised.

The updated version of the Singapore-Asia Taxonomy (SAT) was unveiled on the sidelines of the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, on Wednesday (Nov 11).

Sustainable finance taxonomies set criteria and thresholds for a range of economic activities that would be considered eligible for sustainable and transition financing.

Singapore finalised its own taxonomy in 2023 at COP28 after four rounds of consultations, and is said to be the first globally to lay out criteria for transition activities through the use of a traffic-light system.

Unlike most taxonomies that either classify economic activities that qualify for sustainable financing as “green”, or those that do not qualify as “red”, an “amber” category was introduced to represent transition activities.

This means that carbon-intensive businesses looking to decarbonise can qualify for transition financing if their activities meet the transition criteria laid out in the taxonomy.

## Sectors that are significant to region

This second edition comes after further consultations with the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and the Singapore Sustainable Finance Association (SSFA) over the last year, and reflects broad industry input and suggestions, said Abigail Ng, chief sustainability officer of MAS.

These four sectors were prioritised for their significance to the region’s transition finance needs, noted SSFA in a separate media statement.

The energy-efficiency metrics for data centres located in water-constrained areas were revised to be less stringent, given the trade-offs between energy and water efficiencies.

As for the energy sector, the criteria for activities classified as “amber” are now aligned to an Asean-specific decarbonisation pathway laid out by the *Global Energy and Climate Outlook*.

The maritime sector’s criteria have been revised to align with the International Maritime Organization’s greenhouse-gas strategy, and is also more interoperable with the EU and Asean taxonomy.

Eligibility requirements in iron and steel will no longer mandate specific technologies, such as carbon capture, utilisation and storage. It will instead focus on the activity’s emission intensity, with thresholds set with reference to the International Energy Agency’s 2050 net-zero emissions scenario.

SSFA said that this technology-neutral approach would allow a range of production routes – including upgraded blast furnaces, hydrogen-based direct reduction and others that may emerge – to qualify based on what they achieve rather than the technology they use.

As businesses navigate rising costs, supply chain disruptions and technological change, it remains important that the SAT’s technical screening criteria remain fit for purpose. The changes keeps the SAT aligned with evolving decarbonisation pathways and provide a credible, practical basis for transition finance across Asia, it added.

Additional guidance on how financiers may support enabling activities that are critical to achieving green and transition outcomes, which was released in July last year, will be included as an addendum to the revised taxonomy.

Ng noted that the changes are starting to see real-world application.

The Fund for Energy Efficiency Technologies, which is a blended fund that provides financing to shipowners to install energy-efficiency technologies on their vessels, plans to align its investments with the new transition criteria for the maritime sector.

Set up in Singapore by maritime-focused investor AIM Horizon Investments and the non-profit industry group Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation, the fund will deploy capital into vessel energy-efficiency technologies, such as wind-assisted propulsion systems.

“This shows how a taxonomy can guide capital in hard-to-abate sectors, where reductions often come from incremental yet critical investments in existing assets,” said Ng on Wednesday at the COP31 Singapore Pavilion.

The updates place greater emphasis on climate-mitigation outcomes, align more closely with international frameworks, and expand guidance on transition-enabling activities and equity financing aligned with the taxonomy, she added.

## Carbon markets and insurance

Ng also announced the first two projects that received support from MAS’ carbon market development grant for the financial sector.

Standard Chartered will be expanding its carbon market capabilities across wealth management and corporate banking functions in Singapore. This includes developing carbon-related solutions for private banking clients, as well as small and medium-sized enterprises.

WWF-Singapore is collaborating with Great Eastern to develop and pilot insurance solutions for nature-based carbon projects, supported by the non-profit group’s nature finance platform known as Canopy.

The aim is to de-risk nature-based solutions projects, improve their bankability, and unlock financing for nature conservation across South-east Asia.

The insurance programme will establish a risk-management framework and co-fund insurance premiums for nature-based projects, starting with eligible Canopy projects.

The premiums provide coverage for instances such as project failure, non-delivery of carbon credits, carbon credit eligibility risks, natural catastrophes and climate-related events, said WWF-Singapore in a previous media statement.

On insurance, Ng said that the sector has a distinctive role to play in supporting climate-resilience investments.

“Insurers see risks across the life of an asset, from design and construction to operation and, in some cases, failure. Their expertise can help businesses and financiers manage physical climate risks before they materialise,” she added.

MAS is also exploring developing a “common language” for resilience investments, alongside industry partners.

“We are not looking for a single framework or metric. We want to understand what different approaches measure, how they complement one another, and where the gaps are. Over time, that should make the landscape easier to navigate and support more investment in resilience,” she noted.

stories.title: Synopsys joins NUS tropical data centre cooling consortium
stories.summary: Cooling could account for up to 40% of energy use in tropical data centres, spurring research on cheaper, more efficient systems for AI workloads.
stories.title_zh: Synopsys 加入 NUS 热带数据中心冷却联盟
stories.content:
Wed, 11th Nov 2026 (Yesterday)
Synopsys has joined the Sustainable Tropical Data Centre Testbed Phase 2.0 consortium at the National University of Singapore, adding a semiconductor and engineering software company to a Singapore research effort focused on data centre cooling in tropical conditions.

Led by the National University of Singapore and hosted by its College of Design and Engineering, the consortium will combine engineering simulation, AI-assisted design and reduced-order modelling with physical validation in the testbed.

The partnership addresses a growing challenge as artificial intelligence and high-performance computing drive up power use and heat output in data centres. In tropical markets, high temperatures and humidity make conventional cooling systems less efficient and more energy-intensive.

According to details released by the organisations, cooling can account for up to 40% of a tropical data centre's total energy consumption. That gives operators in Southeast Asia a stronger incentive to test liquid cooling, digital twins and other methods that reduce energy use while maintaining performance.

### Research focus

Initial research will focus on two-phase direct-to-chip cooling for AI accelerators and digital twins for predictive thermal management. The planned workflow uses high-fidelity simulation to study thermal and fluid behaviour before designs are tested in the consortium's physical environment.

Once validated, the simulation results can be used to build reduced-order models, lighter computational models that support digital twin deployment and operational decisions. The collaboration also plans to develop repeatable workflows, case studies and validation methods.

For Synopsys, the project extends its simulation and analysis work into a live research environment focused on data centre infrastructure. Under the collaboration, it will provide software access, technical expertise, training, project mentoring and learning resources.

Brandon Wang, Vice President of Strategic Management, Technology Strategy & New Horizons at Synopsys, said, "At Synopsys, we look beyond today's opportunities to the new horizons that can strengthen our technology long term. Through our Technology Intelligence Centre, our team connects emerging technology shifts with Synopsys capabilities and leading research ecosystems to turn promising ideas into strategic opportunities. Our collaboration with STDCT 2.0 reflects that commitment by bringing our silicon-to-systems engineering capabilities into a real-world environment for sustainable AI infrastructure."

The announcement also reflects Singapore's broader push to improve the efficiency of digital infrastructure as demand for compute capacity grows. The city-state has sought to balance data centre expansion with energy and land constraints, making cooling efficiency a key area of research and investment.

### Testbed model

STDCT 2.0 brings together research institutions, data centre operators and technology providers. Its remit covers energy efficiency, water efficiency, green energy, AI and future data centres, and green computing.

The structure gives academic and industry partners a platform to test ideas under conditions that mirror tropical environments, rather than relying solely on laboratory simulations. That matters because humidity, temperature and denser AI hardware create a different set of constraints from those in cooler regions.

Padmesh Mandloi, Vice President of Applications Engineering for Synopsys Simulation and Analysis APAC at Synopsys, said, "Efficient AI infrastructure requires a clear understanding of interconnected multiscale and multiphysics behavior, from chips to data centers. By combining Ansys multiscale and multiphysics simulation, AI-assisted engineering and surrogate modeling with STDCT 2.0 test data, we can help researchers connect and exchange data across scales, validate designs, and develop scalable cooling and digital twin solutions."

The project highlights the growing overlap between chip design tools, system simulation and data centre operations. As compute clusters become more concentrated, cooling design is no longer just a facilities issue. It increasingly connects component design, rack architecture and site-level thermal management.

Professor Lee Poh Seng, Programme Director of the Sustainable Tropical Data Centre Testbed and Head of the Department of Mechanical Engineering at the College of Design and Engineering at NUS, said, "STDCT 2.0 provides a co-innovation platform to move promising technologies from simulation to validation and towards real-world deployment in tropical data centers. By combining Synopsys' multiphysics simulation, AI-assisted engineering and digital modelling capabilities with our physical testbed, we aim to develop validated, scalable cooling and digital twin solutions for increasingly dense, AI-ready infrastructure in Singapore and across the region."
